## H-0108 · A refused merged claim is thrown away, so the ticket that created the verdict is re-dispatched

- Question: `delivered` refuses most of the merged claims it reads -- a body naming more than one
  issue, a body carrying `Part of` -- and then says nothing about the refusal, so the tick dispatched
  for that issue starts from zero. #235 is the measured cost of exactly that: its own fix arrived as
  PR #238, merged 8 Nov on branch `issue-235` under a body naming eight issues (refused by the count
  arm), and the journal holds `TICK-START unclaimed:235 2026-11-10T22:57:23Z` to `TICK-DONE 23:14:23Z`
  -- seventeen minutes of ceiling to rediscover what the classifier had already read. The ticket asks
  which signal reaches the fix; three candidates were on the table, and the one that looked cheapest
  had to be measured before it could be used.
- Options: trust the head-branch name -- a merged PR whose branch is `issue-N` delivers `#N` | a new
  class that dispatches no tick | a new `undelivered:` channel beside `pr:` and `issue:` | read the
  body's prose for a "does not finish" section | carry the refusal on the row as a marker and tell the
  tick what it means
- Chose: carry the refusal on the row as a marker and tell the tick what it means
- Why: the branch name was measured and lost. Over all 98 merged pull requests `gh pr list --state
  merged --limit 100` returns, a branch of the form `issue-N` would claim 15 closed issues (all already
  closed, so nothing *wrong* closes) and 4 open ones: **#246 four times** -- #254/#255/#256/#258 are all
  branch `issue-246` and #246 is open with a requirement nobody has built, so a branch-shaped rule would
  close the very ticket #277 cites as the case that must not be claimed -- plus #251, which #255's body
  names beside #253 while delivering only #253, whose fix is #257. It is also redundant where it is
  right: 66 of those issues are closed already and 53 are named in a verb-bearing body the classifier
  already reads. `headRefName` is carried on the read anyway, as the note's most useful fact -- a
  reader can go and check out the branch -- and is used to decide nothing. The new-class option lost on
  #235's own lesson: the reason `delivered` is a report and not a suppression is that a row which stops
  dispatching retires work, and the refused set is where the unfinished work demonstrably lives (#246
  is refused by a `Part of` that told the truth; #253 was refused by the count arm at #255 and needed
  the tick that row dispatched, which produced #257 five hours later). A separate `undelivered:`
  channel lost because `triage.sh --tsv` prints only `pr:` and `issue:` and `factory.sh` skips the
  `branch:` channel as a side effect of that filter (`docs/factory.md:493-502`) -- a third silent
  channel is how #251 stayed invisible. Prose lost on the rule this file has repeated since H-0050: a
  body's own sentence about its unfinished parts is a person's claim, and #273 proved one paragraph can
  carry six instructions. What the marker does instead is keep the verdict and hand the refusal down:
  `refused_note` puts `[merged:PR#229 on \`issue-199\` at … -- names it in a 4-issue body]` at the START
  of an `unclaimed` detail, `factory.sh`'s `unclaimed` arm matches the shared literal
  `FACTORY_MERGED_MARK` anchored there -- unanchored would let an issue title buy itself an instruction
  -- and appends the instruction that sends the tick to `gh pr diff` before it writes code. Both
  reopens-veto and the timestamp veto suppress it, because in those two cases a person has already read
  the merged body. Half of this moving without the other half is #272, so `merged_note_docs` pins the
  rule and the reason in `docs/factory.md` and `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` as well.
  What lost. The seventeen minutes are not recoverable, and a tick still runs on a ticket that may be
  finished -- the marker shortens the work, it does not cancel it, which is the price of the option
  that keeps refused work in the queue. The branch name is read and printed but decides nothing, so the
  note is wordier than a branch-only rule would have been. And the marker is one more anchored string
  shared between two shell files, which is a coupling that did not exist before and is pinned by one
  leg rather than by the type system.
  **The checkpoint below is the branch tip, not a `chore(checkpoint): pre-H-0108` commit, and that is a
  lapse rather than a convention.** The rule in `AGENTS.md` and Step 3 of the skill is to take the
  checkpoint before the call; this call was made, and the checkpoint was noticed afterwards. What
  `5cfda8d` does supply is the thing the field is for -- the tree the decision started from, a commit
  that exists and that `git revert` of the effect commit returns to -- so the entry is reversible as
  required, and what is missing is only the empty commit that would have marked the moment. Recorded
  here, dated, because a silently relaxed rule is indistinguishable from one that was never there.
- Effect: `factory/triage.sh` (merged read gains `headRefName`; the `refused_map` scan and
  `refused_note`; the `unclaimed` emit prefixed with the note behind the two vetoes; the header's
  `detail` column and the `--table` example), `factory/common.sh` (`FACTORY_MERGED_MARK`),
  `factory/factory.sh` (the `unclaimed` arm's instruction, plus its class table), `factory/selftest.sh`
  (+30 legs, 417 passed 0 failed against 387 on this same box before the change -- totals are
  box-dependent -- plus two control blocks that print without joining the tally, the shape
  `voided_docs_control` already uses), `docs/factory.md`, `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md`. Read
  back off the live API after the change, not predicted: `./factory/triage.sh --table` prints
  `issue 246 unclaimed [merged:PR#254 on \`issue-246\` at 2026-11-10T01:39:17Z -- a \`Part of\` phrase
  in the same body] TimeoutStopSec reuses the tick ceiling…` -- class unchanged, note present -- and
  `issue 199 delivered merged PR #243 …`, where #199 moved to a sole claim in the hours since the
  probe, so no note. The anchor was tested against a forgery rather than assumed: with the value read
  out of `common.sh`, a detail beginning with the marker hits the arm and a title that merely contains
  `[merged:PR#1]` does not. Two findings came out of writing the legs, both fixed. The fixture shim
  `emit`s a payload file whatever the caller's `--json` asked for, so a read that stopped requesting a
  field would have kept receiving it and every branch-naming leg here would have stayed green -- the
  merged payload is now projected through `with_entries` to the fields actually named, which is what
  `gh` does. And the `jq --slurpfile` in that projection emitted nothing at all until `-n` was added:
  `--slurpfile` binds `$src` and leaves the input empty, so a filter without `-n` runs zero times and
  writes zero bytes with exit 0 -- a silent empty file, the same shape as the `delivered_map=`
  regression `triage.sh:470-479` records, and the reason the new legs assert the note is PRESENT on
  named rows rather than merely absent where it should be. That precedent is the reason the legs exist:
  the scar comment there is `bash -x` showing `delivered_map=` followed by `delivered_map='{}'`, and no
  leg of the day could see an always-empty map.
- Checkpoint: 5cfda8d7781daecab8209d849ac1643044e66844

## H-0109 · The fixture answers fields nobody asked for, so the projection goes into `emit()` and not into another call site

- Question: #279 found both fixture `gh` shims parsing `--json` for one thing only -- telling two
  payloads apart -- and then printing the whole payload file. A shipped read that *stopped* asking for
  a field therefore kept receiving it from the fixture, and every leg asserting something about that
  field stayed green while the read went blind. The issue asked for `H-0108`'s projection lifted out of
  its one branch and paired with a leg that fails when a caller asks for a field the fixture does not
  carry, and it asked for its own plant to be run first. The plant was run first, and it is the whole
  argument: `--json number,title,updatedAt` at `factory/triage.sh:563` reduced to `--json number,title`
  left `bash factory/selftest.sh` at `387 passed, 0 failed` -- identical in tally to the unpunctured
  run, exit 0 -- while the `CLAIM_DEBUG` rows still printed `issue 232 delivered`, a verdict
  `delivered_claim` (triage.sh:509) refuses to render on an empty `updatedAt`. Six payload sites, one
  demonstrated, none of them visible.
- Options: project at each dispatch site, as `H-0108` did for the merged read alone | lift the
  projection into each shim's `emit()` as two separate copies of the rule | one heredoc installed into
  both payload directories and sourced by both `emit()`s, `gh`'s refusal of a field no row carried
  included | leave the fixture alone and pin the field lists with a text check over `triage.sh`
- Chose: one heredoc installed into both payload directories and sourced by both `emit()`s, `gh`'s
  refusal of a field no row carried included
- Why: the first option carries its own refutation, measured in the same week as its fix -- `H-0108`
  projected the merged payload at the merged read, and #279 then counted **six** payload sites still
  served blind, because a rule written at a call site is a rule for that call site. The fourth option
  proves the shipped text says `updatedAt`; it does not prove the read *receives* it, and this class is
  precisely a suite that could not see its own subject (`triage.sh:470-479`'s always-empty
  `delivered_map`, and #242's `${3}` where `${2}` was meant), so a text check is that suite in a
  different costume. Between the middle two the tie-breaks separate them on fewest files and then on
  the reason `H-0108` exists at all: two copies is how one channel got fixed and six did not, and these
  two shims already claim to share every other rule by pointing at each other in comments
  (`CLAIMSHIM`'s write refusal, the process shim's `exit 9`) -- this makes one of those promises
  mechanical instead of aspirational. The refusal is the half the issue named, and it follows the house
  rule for a missing input: refuse rather than proceed. `gh` answers an unknown field with a non-zero
  exit and the field's name, so the fixture does the same, and `labels` -- a field `gh issue list`
  holds for every issue on GitHub and this fixture has never held -- now fails loudly where it used to
  answer no column at all at exit 0, which is indistinguishable from the repository saying "none". That
  is the moment a fixture quietly becomes the specification. `git revert` of the one commit below takes
  all of it back.
  **What lost.** Locality: a reader of one shim no longer sees the projection where the payload is
  printed, and pays a `$here/fields.sh` hop instead -- paid back with a comment at each `emit()` naming
  `install_gh_fields`, which is also where the measurement lives. The honest residue is
  `gh_json_payload`'s empty payload: `gh` checks a field name against its own schema, a fixture has
  only the rows in front of it, and every unlegged read runs against `[]` every pass, so an empty list
  carries no verdict about the field list and is not refused. The check is therefore only as good as a
  planted row, which is why the refusal leg asks the fixture that holds nine. And `H-0108`'s
  site-level branch on `issue-277` becomes redundant beside this one; it is not broken by it --
  re-projecting an already-projected payload to the same field list is the identity -- so whoever
  resolves the shared region is deleting a branch, not correcting one.
- Effect: `factory/selftest.sh` only, plus this entry. Both `emit()`s now answer
  `gh_json_payload <payload> <--json list>`: the document verbatim when no field list was passed (the
  `user` and `graphql` reads, where `gh` has no field contract to obey), otherwise the payload projected
  through `with_entries` with what no row carries refused by name. Eight legs: three that a field not
  named does not come back (the claim-shim, its control, and the same read off the **process** shim,
  which serves the whole supervisor run), two that a field the fixture lacks is refused and one it
  holds is not, and three that run #279's plant end to end -- the mutant's anchor counted before it is
  believed (`proc_mutate`'s rule), then the shipped read one field short must not deliver, then the
  shipped file as it ships must. Measured on rodney-9950x, btrfs, one `bash factory/selftest.sh` per
  row, the same fixture as `H-0100`'s table: unpunctured `395 passed, 0 failed` (was 387; eight legs,
  15.1 s -> 16.0 s); the plant with this fix in `375 passed, 20 failed`, exit 1, against the `0 failed`
  the same plant produced above; and the fix with its projection neutralised in both `emit()`s --
  everything else left in place -- `391 passed, 4 failed`, which is four of the eight saying the old
  answer out loud. `make check-shell` clean, 0.10.0 over 28 scripts. No `.go` file is touched, so no
  mutant anchor moves and `scripts/check-mutations.py` is not the gate this change needs (#1048's
  surface is `.go` and `.tmpl`).
  **Corrected at the merge, 11 Nov, and not quietly.** This entry said the measurement ran on
  `btrfs`; it copied that from #279's table and from `H-0100` instead of reading it. `H-0104`, which

  What that class costs a count is `H-0045`'s measured ±1 -- one exclude-file leg flips its verdict

## H-0116 · The review poke addressed one named person, and a review request is a question put to whoever can answer it

- Id: this entered the harness log as `H-0055` on `issue-241`, and `H-0056` as its second entry. Both numbers are published on `main` as other decisions -- `H-0055` there is *A dispatch carried the review's timestamp and not its text*, `H-0056` is *The supervisor runs whatever is checked out in its worktree* -- and a merged entry's id never moves, so these two, unmerged, yielded. They took `H-0116` and `H-0117`, the first ids no ref held at the merge (`origin/main` at `H-0114`, `origin/issue-237` at `H-0115`), read from `factory/next-decision-id.sh` rather than by eye. The two commits that made these decisions keep `Decision: H-0055` and `Decision: H-0056` in their messages: rewriting an in-flight branch is forbidden here, so the mapping lives in this line and `git log --grep='Decision: H-0116'` will not find the work.

- Question: #241 says the `needs_reviewer` arm asks `hermesvicowa` and should ask `vicowa-botworks/cinemaitor` -- "ask the team, not a member, because we do not know who is online at what time". Does the poke change addressee, and what happens to the two readers that decide whether anybody has been asked at all?
- Options: add `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM` beside the individual and keep asking the individual by default | make the team the default and keep the individual as the override, one target with a kind | keep one variable and guess from its value whether it names a person or a team | ask the team and cancel whatever individual request is already on the list | change only the documentation and leave the poke asking a login
- Chose: make the team the default and keep the individual as the override, one target with a kind
- Why: the default this file carried for four days was justified by the wrong kind of evidence. "The account that has approved every PR in this repository's history" (measured 4 Nov: reviews on #195, #197, #201, #203, #206) is a prediction about who answered the past, and a request is not a prediction -- it is a question put to everyone who could answer it. A team request notifies every member and the first one online replies; an individual request waits for one particular person to appear. The clock on that needs stating, because it cuts against the change: #240 is `MERGED`, `mergedAt 19:50:20Z` on 8 Nov, carrying four reviews and all four from `hermesvicowa` (18:19:17Z, 18:41:12Z, 19:06:38Z, approved 19:49:56Z), and its request list reads empty on the read taken while this branch was being written. The two readings either side of the ask -- that login alone before, the team alone after -- were taken earlier the same day and cannot be re-taken now, because the pull request that carried them has merged; they are kept as readings, not offered as current state. What the day does not support is in `Effect:` below: the honest reading is that the same account reviewed it anyway. The team argument is one argument on the endpoint this script already posts to and already reads back -- the verb that moved #240 was a post with `team_reviewers[]`, then a delete with `reviewers[]` -- so no new permission and no new route, and `.opencode/opencode.jsonc:72-86` already records that the raw call is denied to a tick (`:120`) precisely so that the actor making this ask is `factory_request_review` in factory.sh rather than an agent. Tie-break 1 decided between options one and two: both notify the team, but a default is a guess about a repository nobody has asked yet, and option one keeps guessing wrong for every repository in the org while option two's failure is one variable in a unit. Tie-break 4 is what refuses option three -- guessing a kind from a value cannot be undone after a 404 that was really a slug spelled as a login -- and this org has the exact collision on the record: `slug=cinemaitor`, `name=cinemAItor` (the org team listing, 8 Nov), so a case-sensitive display name is a plausible value that fails. Option four is a second decision the issue did not ask for and is H-0117. Two things the work found that the issue did not name. (a) The classifier was the other half of the bug: `triage.sh` decided "nobody was asked" from the `users` list alone, and a team request arrives in `teams[]` with `users[]` empty -- so every team-requested pull request would read `needs_reviewer` forever, the arm would call the poke, the post would 422, the users-only read-back would deny the request exists, and the journal would fill with `POKE-FAILED` lines about a request sitting right there. Fixed by making both readers run one shared program (`$JQ_REQUESTED_LIST` and `$JQ_REQUESTED_HOLDS`, `common.sh`), the same reason `JQ_CHECKS` exists. The team's name is taken as `slug`, then `login`, then `name`, with the `org/` prefix stripped and the comparison case-folded, because `slug` is what the current REST schema makes required and the other two are the spellings that field has carried; that is read from the public schema, not from a payload this machine captured, because the raw API call is denied to a tick whole by D-0013 -- so `selftest.sh` carries a leg per spelling instead of a capture. (b) `factory_request_review` printed `$FACTORY_REVIEWER` in every journal line whatever it had posted, so a team request would have been journalled as asking a login; the target now comes from `factory_review_target` and the post, the read-back, the journal and the `--dry-run` echo all print that one string. `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM=${VAR-default}` without the colon is load-bearing: the documented override is `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM=` and the colon form would refill the empty value and keep asking cinemaitor -- the same absent-versus-false distinction #873 makes for a config key. `factory_preflight`'s self-review refusal had to follow the target rather than the variable, because the person running the supervisor is very likely a member of the team it asks, and the unconditioned check refused to start the supervisor over a request it would never have made.
- Checkpoint: b4c52f071cba3e66e79320b3139585f5ecbf8610
- Effect: `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM` plus `factory_review_target` (`common.sh`), the target-shaped post, read-back and journal in `factory_request_review` (`factory.sh:170`), `$JQ_REQUESTED_*` shared with `triage.sh:248`, the second `Environment=` line generated into the unit (`install-timer.sh`), and `docs/factory.md` carrying the rule with the classifier table's row now reading "neither `users` nor `teams`". Legs 179 to 200 in this commit and 201 at the head of the branch, 0 failed at both -- CI had not seen the push when this was written, so those numbers are this box and H-0054's history says the two can differ. Six controls stand behind them. Four print the line that says the leg they stand for goes red over the reverted copy: the addressee put back to a login, the no-target guard made unable to fire, the preflight guard blinded to the target, the classifier put back to the `users` list. The fifth is a leg of its own -- a read-back put back to `users` only, which has to report failure about a request plainly in the payload -- and the sixth, a revoke planted after the post, is H-0117's. Three fixture bugs surfaced by writing these legs, all fixed here: a `case` pattern containing a space ends the pattern and kills the shim at parse time; the api dispatch read the third argument, which is the literal `--jq` in a `gh api` call, so no api arm could ever match and every one of those reads exited 9 and handed the caller `api_get`'s default -- an empty list, indistinguishable from a correct answer. That index arrived with 18ab007 (`git log -S`), #235's section, so the merged-claim legs have been green since then without ever being asked for a review payload; the proof it was never load-bearing is that the same suite read 179 passed, 0 failed the whole time, and the proof the read matters now is that putting the index back at this head turns exactly the six classifier legs red (195 passed, 6 failed) while leaving the poke legs alone, because the poke has its own shim. Nothing pins the shim's argument index with a leg, so the sentence before this one is how it was checked. And the poke shim dumped its payload instead of running the caller's own filter, which made a correct read-back look like a failure and let a wrong one look like a pass. What lost, as measured: the individual default, so a repository that wants a login asked must set `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM=` and no leg catches a unit that forgets; and #240's own day does not show a second reviewer appearing -- all four reviews that evening came from `hermesvicowa` (18:19:17Z, 18:41:12Z, 19:06:38Z, approved 19:49:56Z, merged 19:50:20Z) and `cinemaitor` holds two members, one of them that account and the other the org's own machine user (the team's member list, read earlier the same day -- the raw call is withheld from a tick by D-0013, so it is a reading kept from earlier rather than one re-taken at this head). The claim this entry rests on is therefore about reach and about the issue's explicit instruction, not about an observed new name, and the day a team review is answered by a second human is the day this choice earns its keep in a measurement rather than an argument. Also unpaid, on the record: no leg proves the spelling GitHub actually sends, because the raw API is withheld from a tick (D-0013) -- the tolerance is a schema reading with three legs behind it, and a fourth spelling would need one; and `factory_preflight`'s runtime term is satisfied in this section by the `$claim_bin/opencode` stub (H-0054), which the new legs inherit rather than re-test. Re-measured on the merge with `origin/main` (163 commits, trunk at `075dede`): `factory/selftest.sh: 460 passed, 0 failed`, and the 22 `claim_leg` calls in this branch's #241 section are unchanged in number -- the 179/200/201 tallies above are the pre-merge base and are kept as the record of that tree, not as a claim about this one. Four collisions, none of them in the shipped behaviour, resolved in that merge: `#272` had rewritten the same `requested=` line in `triage.sh` to keep the whole `/reviews` array, so the shared program was re-pointed at main's shape rather than the old three-field projection; `#272` fixed the same `gh api` argument-index bug in the claim fixture independently, and its comment carries both stories because an unreachable fixture arm fails as an empty queue and not as an error; two fixture helpers collided by name and the trunk spelling won (`claim_requested` -> `claim_reviewers`, `CLAIM_TRIAGE` -> `claim_script`, the latter reset in `claim_reset` so a control's mutant classifier still cannot leak into the next leg); and one of main's own legs asserts the journal line this change renames -- `voided_asked` expected `WOULD-POKE pr:269 request review from someoneelse`, which the shipped default no longer prints, so it expects `request review from team cinemaitor` and `ask_dispatch` now pins `FACTORY_REVIEWER_TEAM` to the shipped default for the reason `FACTORY_OPENCODE` already gives in that file (inherited, the leg is green or red on what the operator exports). A fifth was documentation only: `docs/factory.md`'s #272 section quotes `POKED pr:269 requested review from hermesvicowa` from 10 Nov, and the quotation is kept and labelled as the older spelling rather than rewritten, because the same event now reads `asked team cinemaitor` and a doctored quotation is worth less than a dated one. Dated correction at `H-0127`, 11 Nov: the line cites above drifted after the merge -- `factory_request_review` was at `factory/factory.sh:245`, the shared requested-reviewers read at `factory/triage.sh:346`, the default and target at `factory/common.sh:83`/`:89`, the unit line at `factory/install-timer.sh:395`, and the documentation row at `docs/factory.md:329`; the original 8 Nov citations are kept as what they measured then.

## H-0117 · A review request the poke did not make stays where it is: adding a team cancels nothing

- Id: this entered the harness log as `H-0056` on `issue-241`; see `H-0116`'s `Id:` line for why both numbers moved and which commits still carry the old trailers.

- Question: asking `cinemaitor` on #240 left `hermesvicowa` on the same list -- the live read at 22:04Z was a user request and a team request both outstanding, though the read-back two hours later finds the pull request merged with an empty list, which `Effect:` records. Does the poke cancel an individual request it did not make, and who owns that call?
- Options: cancel every individual request as soon as the team is asked | leave it -- the poke adds and never removes | cancel only requests the poke itself made, named by a ledger marker | escalated to a maintainer
- Chose: leave it -- the poke adds and never removes
- Why: the owner was asked directly, at 22:04Z on 8 Nov, with the live state and both consequences named, and declined to hold the decision: "this is exactly the decision I shouldn't have to make. Tie-breaks 4 and 5 say stop, but stopping is the thing that costs the most here -- every unattended PR in the queue is holding a request someone else made while the question sits." So it is decided here, on the record, one `git revert` from being unmade. Given an explicit refusal to reserve the call, stopping would itself be the choice with the biggest footprint: it leaves the queue holding an unanswered question and delivers nothing. Tie-break 4 then decides it -- the action that keeps every option open wins. Adding a team is reversible in one call, and the state after is a superset of what anybody asked for. Cancelling a person destroys a fact this script did not create and cannot reconstruct: who asked, and why they thought that person owed this pull request an answer. Tie-break 5, the asymmetry this repository already encodes as `allow_squash_merge=false` and `allow_rebase_merge=false`, forbids the destructive default; it does not forbid the conservative one. The blast radius of leaving it is one extra notification to somebody who may not owe the review -- bounded, self-limiting the moment they review or decline, and the two kinds of request are counted separately so a review from either side clears the gate. The blast radius of the alternative is a human's routing decision silently revoked by a machine, with no record of the intent. The third option is what to build if this ever actually costs something -- it answers both halves exactly -- and it was not built now because a marker is a second writer to the per-PR ledger, which is H-0026's problem to solve, because the poke already stamps `last-poke` per pull request and a second file per request buys a new way to be out of date, and because nothing measured in #241 asks for it: #240 is the only row in the queue where the two kinds coexist.
- Checkpoint: b4c52f071cba3e66e79320b3139585f5ecbf8610
- Effect: `factory_request_review` has no revoke path on either the success arm or the already-holding arm, and the legs prove both the absence and its teeth -- one asserts no delete request reaches the API after a clean ask and after a 422, the other plants a revoke immediately after the `POKED` line and goes red on the same assertion. What lost: the poke has no way to tidy a list it did not create. Nothing in the queue is holding both kinds at the head of this branch, measured rather than assumed: #240, the row the question was raised on, reads `state: MERGED` with `mergedAt 19:50:20Z` and `reviewRequests: []`, which puts the 22:04Z observation two hours AFTER the merge timestamp -- so that state cannot be reproduced from here and this option was chosen on the owner's reading plus the rule, not on a state still on the board. The open queue at the same moment is #245 holding one individual request (`hermesvicowa`) and #243 holding none. That is also why the legs are the whole artifact here: they pin a behaviour no live row currently exercises. And if the org later decides a stale individual request is noise worth clearing, the fix is not just the delete but the marker that knows which requests are the poke's -- the ledger marker named above is the thing to build, and this entry is the thing to read before building it. Re-read on the merge with `origin/main` (`075dede`): the two legs that pin this still pass, at `factory/selftest.sh: 460 passed, 0 failed`, and no row in the open queue holds both kinds of request at that head -- the read this entry rests on is still the 8 Nov one and still two hours after #240's merge timestamp, which is said here rather than smoothed, because the option was chosen on the rule and the owner's reading, not on a state anyone can re-take.

## H-0118 · The reaping read is the unit's own journal, not `Result=`, because `Result=` is wrong on the polarity that matters

- Question: `#246` shipped two deadlines in #254 and left the second half open -- the ticket says
  "the teardown itself must be visible: the unit's `SubState` during the hold, and the residue
  `Result=timeout` afterwards". Both of those signals were measured on this box on 11 Nov, against a
  reproduction of the fault and against the real unit, and the suggested one fails on the case the
  ticket was written about. What was wanted is a reading of "how did the last pass get reaped?" that
  a person gets from `factory.sh --status`, the one command the ticket says a person types.

  Measured, all of it on this box, systemd 259.9-0ubuntu0.1, user manager for uid 1000:

  | activation | main exit | hold | `Result=` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | control, nothing leaked | 4 | 0.3 ms | `exit-code` |
  | one `trap '' TERM` descendant, `TimeoutStopSec=60` | 4 | **60.194 s** | `exit-code` |
  | same, `TimeoutStopSec=20`, paired `OnUnitInactiveSec=10s` | 4 | **20.135 s**; next pass started **30.4 s** after the previous one's last line | `exit-code` |
  | the factory unit, 11 Nov 00:56 -- `winedevice.exe` again | 0 | **60.18 s** | `timeout` |
  | the factory unit, 8 Nov 22:18 -- the 91-minute outage | 4 | 4084 s, ended by a hand-escalated kill | `exit-code` |

  So `Result=timeout` appears when the pass exited *cleanly* and `Result=exit-code` when it did not,
  on held teardowns and clean ones alike. `Result` records what the main process returned, not what
  the stop path waited for. It is right on tonight's clean-exit hold and wrong on 8 Nov -- the exact
  incident named in the ticket, whose pass exited 4 -- so it would have answered "nothing to see" to
  the only question this line exists to answer. `SubState=stop-sigterm` is a true signal and was
  verified live (`SubState=stop-sigterm TasksCurrent=10 MainPID=0` is printed by the new `live:`
  clause), but it is a window of one `TimeoutStopSec` inside a cadence of ten minutes: nothing whose
  attention is not already on the screen sees it.

- Options: `systemctl --user show -p Result -p SubState`, as the issue suggests, as the source | poll
  `SubState` from a watcher, so the answer is live whenever someone asks | parse the unit's journal for
  the two systemd lines that name an escalation and the unit's own last line as the moment the work
  stopped, with the live manager read appended as a clause that is dropped when the bus does not
  answer | read systemd's own lifetime figure, `Consumed ... over <n> wall clock`
- Chose: parse the unit's journal for the two systemd lines that name an escalation and the unit's own
  last line as the moment the work stopped, with the live manager read appended as a clause that is
  dropped when the bus does not answer

- Why: the journal keeps the two facts apart and is readable by anyone, including a tick, with no
  grant. `State 'stop-sigterm' timed out. Killing.` and `Killed unit cgroup ... with SIGKILL on
  client request.` say not just that it was held but by what, which is the difference between
  "shorten the ceiling" and "go reap it by hand" -- and the second is a manager write, so the
  sentence has to name it rather than reach for it. The hold's start had to come from the unit's own
  stdout and not from systemd: for a pass that exits 0 there is no `Main process exited` line at all,
  measured on tonight's incident, and a read filtered `-t systemd` timed that 60-second hold as 0s
  until it was widened. It is therefore an overestimate by whatever a silent pass does on its way out,
  which is the conservative direction for an alarm. The three that lost, with what killed each: the
  manager read mis-polarises -- `Result` records what the main process returned, not what the stop path
  waited for, so it is right on tonight's clean-exit hold and wrong on 8 Nov, the incident named in the
  ticket -- and a tick is refused the manager on principle (`.opencode/opencode.jsonc`: "systemctl is
  the wrong verb here, whatever the subcommand"), so a read that needs the bus cannot be the read the
  harness makes about itself; a watcher polling `SubState` answers only while someone is watching, which
  is the failure mode #248 was filed about, and it costs a daemon; `Consumed ... over <n> wall clock` is
  the activation's whole life, and the number wanted is the part after the pass stopped working -- 17
  minutes of real work and 60 seconds of freeze are one figure to that line.

- Checkpoint: 97b28e867bb5b5c0d7c68ae050591f92f5a6f193

- Effect: `factory/common.sh` gains `factory_reap_lines`, `factory_reap_lastword`, `factory_reap_read`
  and `factory_reap_line` beside `factory_timer_state`, plus `FACTORY_REAP_NOTICE_SECS` (5 s, three
  orders of magnitude away from the 0.3 ms of a clean reaping) and `FACTORY_REAP_TAIL`;
  `factory/factory.sh --status` prints `reaping:` between `unit:` and `trees:`. Against the live
  journal of the real unit on this box it prints `HELD 1m00s to the stop deadline -- a descendant of
  the pass ignored SIGTERM ... Ended 25m22s ago.` for the 00:56 incident, with the measured truth being
  00:56:06.070895 to 00:57:06.252797, 60.18 s. It does not merge or publish anything; merging stays
  the supervisor's, and the transient units this measurement created in the user manager are left for
  a human to remove, because removing one is a manager write (`plock246-*`, named in the pull request).
- Correction (`H-0119`, 11 Nov, on #283's red `verify`): what was decided here is unchanged; what was
  wrong is the record of it, and it shipped. As committed at `a99762e` the four options above sat as an
  indented bullet list under `Options:`, which is not this log's grammar --
  `scripts/check-decisions.py:218` splits the field on `|`, so a nested list folds into ONE option and

  rejections moved out of the option text into `Why:` the way every other entry in this log carries
  them, and the checkpoint written as the sha its heading names. Corrected in a dated line rather than

  body` carries a "Measurements (`H-0118`)" heading and the five-row table -- and a silently corrected

## H-0124 · The reaping read had two ways to run out of input and one of them printed a zero -- both answer unknown now, in two different sentences

- Question: #283's review names this as the polarity follow-on inside the same function it filed as
  blocking: when no process line is found, `factory_reap_read` fell back to `work=$term`, measuring
  the hold from the terminal line to the terminal line. Measured here through the `PATH` stub the legs
  will use, at `fd36792`, on transcripts with systemd's lines and nothing else -- because `-t systemd`
  excludes the unit's stdout, that is what this function's own stream always looks like:

  | the finished activation's stream | before | after |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `Starting`, `State 'stop-sigterm' timed out. Killing.`, `Failed to start` | `0 deadline` → `HELD 0s to the stop deadline -- a descendant of the pass ignored SIGTERM` | rc 2 |
  | `Starting`, `Finished`, `Consumed` | `0 clean` → `reaped in 0s; the unit has been inactive for 6h08m` | rc 2 |

  So the alarm printed a hold of zero seconds for a teardown it had not measured, and the healthy-case
  sentence was one of the two outputs. The fallback was written as "nothing better available", but
  after `H-0123` there IS a better source and it has already been asked: `factory_reap_lastword`
  returned 1, which means the journal does not say when the work stopped. Is not-saying a fact about
  the unit, or a zero to print?

- Options: keep the fallback and call the printed hold a lower bound | refuse with a third exit code
  and its own sentence | refuse with the same rc 1 the no-terminal-line arm already returns | raise
  `FACTORY_REAP_TAIL` and the stub window until a process line is always inside them
- Chose: refuse with a third exit code and its own sentence
- Why: every other error this function can make runs upward -- an unread work line, a bounded window,
  a pass whose chattiness pushed lines out of the tail all overestimate the hold, which is the
  direction an alarm wants. This one runs to zero, and zero is the value the healthy case prints, so
  the failure is indistinguishable from the thing it is meant to distinguish; `H-0118` chose the
  journal over `Result=` for exactly this kind of reason and `#228` is the polarity in general -- a
  read that failed is not evidence of the clean state. A lower bound (option one) is refused because
  the number would sit in the same slot with the same typography and the only difference would be one
  qualifier inside a sentence an operator reads once; this repository's refusals say what they mean in
  their own sentence, the way `unknown` does here already. Option three is refused because the two
  arms send a reader to different places: "no finished activation in the window" is a reason to look
  at the timer, "it finished and the journal cannot say when its work stopped" is a reason to look at
  the unit's stdout, and `factory_reap_line` has the manager's live state in the same line to make
  either readable. Option four is refused on a measurement rather than a principle: the 08:44 pass
  wrote 11 `DELIVERED` lines inside 60 ms, so bursts are how the arm gets reached in the first place,
  and no finite window promises a line -- it only trades a silent unknown for a slower read. Tie-break
  4: one file, no new tool, no manager call. Tie-break 5: `git revert` of the effect commit restores
  the optimistic arm whole. What lost: a real hold can now be reported as unknown when the unit logs
  nothing at all, and unknown does not alarm anybody -- mitigated only by the fact that the same line
  carries the manager's live substate, which does know `activating` from `failed`; and a helper's exit
  status now carries meaning in three values, which every future caller has to read, pinned by a leg
  and not by a type.
- Checkpoint: fd36792
- Effect: `factory/common.sh` only. The fallback returns 2 instead of inventing a start point, a
  work-stamp `date` cannot parse returns 2 for the same reason, `factory_reap_read`'s contract names
  both codes and what each asserts, `FACTORY_REAP_TAIL`'s promise is symmetric now ("either END of the
  measurement"), and `factory_reap_line` captures the pipeline's status rather than flattening it to
  an empty string, printing a second unknown sentence for rc 2. Witness, the two transcripts above at
  this commit: rc 2 both times, `HELD 0s to the stop deadline` and `reaped in 0s` both gone, the new
  sentence reads `... finished, but nothing in the tail says when its work stopped ... so the hold is
  unread, not zero`. The live journal is unmoved: `factory_reap_lines | factory_reap_read` still
  answers `hold=60` for the 08:44 activation, because there the pass's own line exists.
  `bash factory/selftest.sh` 447 passed 0 failed -- unchanged again, and for the same reason: no leg
  reads any of this yet; the legs are the next commit, and until they exist both this arm and
  `H-0123`'s exclusion can be edited back with the suite green. Nothing merges or publishes.

## H-0125 · The legs replay a transcript through a stub `journalctl` with two personalities, and the second one is the only thing that can tell a read which owns its window from one that outsources it

- Question: #283's review calls `H-0123`'s move of `factory_reap_lastword` to top level "a
  precondition for the leg, not a cosmetic", and asks for three: the 11 Nov transcript, a control, and
  one whose window holds a manager line in an EARLIER second than the terminal line -- the shape that
  would have caught the bracket typo. #246 says the same thing from the other side: "the suite must
  pass standalone with no host journal at all", so the legs cannot read this box. What is replayable,
  given that `factory_reap_lines` and `factory_reap_lastword` each shell out to `journalctl` and the
  parsing depends on how `journalctl` renders a line?

- Options: fixtures under `$work` and a `PATH` stub, run in both a flag-honouring and a
  flag-ignoring personality | boot a real journal into a `systemd-run --scope -p` sandbox and read it
  with the real `journalctl` | stub `factory_reap_lines` only and hand `factory_reap_read` a pipe, so
  no subprocess runs at all | drive `factory.sh --status` and assert on its prose

- Chose: fixtures under `$work` and a `PATH` stub, run in both a flag-honouring and a flag-ignoring
  personality
- Why: option three is the tempting one and it is a trap -- it exercises the `case` and nothing else,
  because the rendering (`<stamp> <host> <comm>[pid]: <message>`, which the parse splits on `"]: "`)
  and the second `journalctl` call both live in `factory_reap_lastword`. Option two is refused on
  cost and on a hard dependency: it needs a manager, and #246's whole premise is that the queue must
  be diagnosable where the manager is not answering. Option four asserts on the sentence rather than
  the number, which is how `H-0118`'s table got quoted as evidence for a reading nobody had tested.
  The second personality is the part worth the entry. A stub that honours `--until` makes the
  truncation of the anchor invisible: the read looks correct because `journalctl` did the bounding,
  and `H-0123`'s point is that this box's `journalctl` truncates to the resolution of the stamp it is
  handed (`--until 2026-11-11T08:45:09+00:00` stopping the window at 08:45:08.999972). `RP_DUMB=1`
  implements neither `--until` nor `-n`, so every leg that reports the same shape both ways is
  asserting the read survives a backend that does nothing for it. Measured, four plants against
  `factory/common.sh`, each restored by `cp` and confirmed byte-identical: the inert `(` exclusion
  turns SIX legs red including the live one; truncating each stamp to its own second in
  `factory_reap_usec` turns three red; deleting the read's own comparison
  `($1 "") > (until "")` turns exactly one red, `reap: nothing after the terminal line counts`, which
  is the leg written for it; the `work=$term` fallback turns one red, `reap: no worker line is
  unknown, not zero`. Two of the four were found by writing the fixtures rather than by the review,
  and both are in the shipped text now. (a) The review's suggested `systemd\[[0-9]+\]`, applied as a
  substring match anywhere in the line -- which is what `H-0123` shipped -- over-drops: a line from
  the UNIT whose message quotes a manager line contains ` systemd[4485]: ` too, and on the
  `reap: the exclusion matches a real rendering` transcript that form answers rc 2, unknown, for a
  teardown the transcript plainly does describe. `factory_reap_line` prints such a quote itself
  (`systemd: "State 'stop-sigterm' timed out. Killing."`), so this is not a hypothetical author. The
  exclusion is now anchored to the field the author occupies, `/^[^ ]+ +[^ ]+ +systemd\[[0-9]+\]: /`,
  which is also what the parse at `factory/common.sh:592` already assumes -- it requires `"]: "` in
  the line and skips the line otherwise, which is why the reviewer's literal `systemd(4485): `
  rendering was never a journal rendering and why the paren fixture this section first drafted
  measured nothing: with parens the parser drops those lines before any filter runs. (b) The `case`
  in `factory_reap_read` matches its cause sentences as substrings of the message, so a unit line
  quoting `Failed with result 'timeout'.` sets the verdict word to `deadline` -- left as shipped,
  because the quote does report the cause and changing it is a different claim than this entry's; the
  fixture quotes a `Consumed` line instead and says so. Tie-break 4: no new tool, no manager, one
  file plus the functions already written. Tie-break 5: `git revert` of the effect commit deletes the
  section and nothing else. What lost: the stub accepts and discards `-u`, `-t`, `-o` and `--utc`, so
  a leg cannot catch a wrong flag -- a missing `--utc` or a plain `-o short-iso` is caught only by
  the live leg, and that leg prints `skip` on a machine with no user journal, which is the case #246
  says must pass; and each transcript now costs up to two subprocess pairs, thirteen invocations for
  eight legs.
- Checkpoint: f2dc6b1
- Effect: `factory/selftest.sh` gains eight legs between the skill-`--jq` section and the tally
  (447 passed 0 failed at the checkpoint, 455 passed 0 failed here, the delta exactly this section,
  `bash factory/selftest.sh` exit 0), and `factory/common.sh` gains the anchored exclusion plus the
  docstring that says why an anchored match and not a substring one. Fixtures are this box's real
  stamps -- 60.133 s, 0.517 ms, 5.2 s -- with the unit renamed `plrev283b.service`, the name #283's
  review used. `python3 scripts/check-scripts.py` clean, `shellcheck -S style` clean on both files,
  `python3 scripts/check-mutations.py` 847 mutants apply and compile. The checkpoint itself is a
  finding: the first attempt at it, `70e6797`, was made with `git add -A` and so committed the effect
  INTO the checkpoint -- the "checkpoint taken afterwards records the state the decision produced"
  failure `AGENTS.md` names, caught before any push (the branch was 5 ahead, nothing published),
  undone with `git reset --soft HEAD~1` plus `git restore --staged` so the effect returned to the
  working tree, and re-taken as the empty `f2dc6b1` whose parent is `88451d9`; `70e6797` survives in
  the reflog. `make verify` is not run by this entry and is owed before the branch is pushed. Nothing
  merges or publishes: merging is the supervisor's.

## H-0126 · The live half of the reaping line threw away the labels that make it readable, and printed the healthy sentence for a unit the manager never loaded

- Question: #283's review's second non-blocking row, measured independently by whoever wrote it:
  `factory_unit_state` pipes `systemctl show` through `sed -n 's/^[A-Za-z]*=//p'`, so the clause reads
  `parental-lockout-factory.service inactive dead success [not set]`; `systemctl show` answers in its
  own order rather than the requested one (asked `ActiveState SubState TasksCurrent Result`, received
  `ActiveState SubState Result TasksCurrent`), so the bare values are positionally ambiguous as well
  as unlabelled; asked about `no-such-unit.service` -- a unit the manager has never loaded -- the same
  four properties answer the same `inactive dead success [not set]`, which is the live half of a
  healthy `reaping:` line about a unit that does not exist; and `H-0118`'s `Effect:` says the clause
  prints `SubState=stop-sigterm TasksCurrent=10 MainPID=0` when `MainPID` was never in the `-p` list.
  Is a clause that must be memorised to be read an acceptable reading of the one field that can see a
  hold while it is happening, and which property tells `not-found` from idle?

- Options: keep the strip and ask one property per call so the order is the one asked | keep the strip
  and add `LoadState` as a fifth bare value | print `key=value` as answered, and ask for `LoadState`
  and `MainPID` as well | leave the clause alone and correct `H-0118` to say it never carried `MainPID`
- Chose: print `key=value` as answered, and ask for `LoadState` and `MainPID` as well
- Why: the strip costs the reader a lookup table and buys nothing -- the clause is the end of a
  sentence, not a field a program parses, and a program that did want to grep it wants exactly
  `SubState=stop-sigterm`, which the stripped form cannot express. One call per property (option one)
  buys an order nobody asked for at six times the manager calls, on the one read whose docstring says
  it must stay off the bus when the bus is contested. Labels are also the only fix that survives the
  order not being contractual: `systemctl show` owes nobody the sequence, so pairing each value with
  its key is what makes the order stop mattering rather than making it correct by luck. `LoadState` is
  the property that separates "never loaded" from "idle", and the distinction is this file's own
  standing argument -- #228 is "a read that failed is not the clean state", and a live half that says
  the healthy words about a unit nothing can load is that failure in the half the review could not
  raise as blocking. Option four was the cheap way out and it is refused: `MainPID=0` beside
  `TasksCurrent=10` -- main process gone, cgroup not empty -- is the 8 Nov outage in two fields, the
  pair `H-0118` measured and the pair an operator needs, so making the claim true is worth more than
  documenting it false. Tie-break 3 is unchanged and deliberate: one `systemctl` call, `|| out=''`, the
  clause vanishes when the bus is unreachable and the journal half still answers. Tie-break 5: one
  revertable commit, nothing published. What lost: the clause grows from 31 to 102 characters for the
  shipped unit (measured here, both against the live manager), and anyone scripting against the
  stripped form loses it -- there is no such script, `factory_reap_line` is the only caller. The
  legs' stub had to learn to read its own `-p`
  arguments: a stub that answered the whole property set whatever it was asked let a dropped `-p` look
  present, and that is exactly the arm `reap: not-loaded is not healthy` exists to notice -- found by
  planting it, not by reading.
- Checkpoint: 7221336
- Effect: `factory/common.sh` (`factory_unit_state` and the comment above it) and `factory/selftest.sh`
  (three legs, `reap: the last-words read is reachable`, `reap: the live half names its keys`,
  `reap: not-loaded is not healthy`; the stub `systemctl` now answers only the properties it is asked
  for, in the order systemd answers rather than the order asked). `bash factory/selftest.sh` 458 passed
  0 failed against 455 at the checkpoint -- the delta is these three -- and `shellcheck -S style` clean
  on both files. Four plants, each restored by `cp` and confirmed byte-identical: `factory_reap_lastword`
  moved back inside `factory_reap_read` (the `0a3939d` shape) turns exactly one leg red and the leg
  prints the reviewer's own number, `rc=127`; `sed -n 's/^[A-Za-z]*=//p'` restored turns two red; `-p
  LoadState` removed turns two red; `-p MainPID` removed turns one red. #283's Blocking 2 is therefore
  now pinned rather than merely fixed: at `050f25d` the move was real and no guard measured it, which
  is the same difference between a fix and a guard that this log keeps writing about. `docs/factory.md`
  is corrected in the same push, one commit later, so the page's owed-thing paragraph and the
  measurement that retires it are separable: it now owes only the manager write, carries the
  five-row hold table, and says where every number on the `reaping:` line comes from. No dependency, no
  security property, no publish, no deletion. Nothing here merges -- merging is the supervisor's.

  8 Nov reading | change the default and build the guard in the same decision | leave the default and escalate
  because `gh api` is denied to a tick

  beside `H-0116`'s 8 Nov reading

## H-0129 · The pass writes down what the previous pass cost the queue, because a 60-second window is not a thing anybody is asked about

- Question: #283 shipped this read into `factory.sh --status` and its own body named what was left: "the
  pass path does not yet log a held teardown to the harness journal, so #248-style watching still needs
  someone to run `--status`". Is a fact that exists only as the answer to a question *delivered*, when the
  window it is true in is one `TimeoutStopSec` wide -- 60 s against a ten-minute cadence, in a substate
  nobody has open -- and the failure it reports is the one where every other reading says healthy?
  Measured the morning this entry was written, with the read in the tree and the line not: five activations
  on this box held the queue about a minute each (08:05:36->08:06:36, 08:21:08->08:22:09,
  08:44:08->08:45:09, 09:20:42->09:21:42, 09:41:42->09:42:42, `last word -> terminal stamp`, every one
  `winedevice.exe`, every one ending `Failed with result 'timeout'`), and `grep -c REAP` over the journal
  those five passes wrote answered `0`.
- Options: leave it in `--status` and let #248's watcher poll it | write the mark on every pass, journal
  only, one line | the same plus a ledger stamp so each hold is written exactly once across passes |
  `WatchdogSec=` with a ping from inside the pass | a journald-side companion unit reading the previous
  activation's `Result=`
- Chose: write the mark on every pass, journal only, one line
- Why: option one is the state this branch inherited and it is the #249/#260 argument refused in the
  present tense -- nobody asks a timer a question, and the 9 Nov note on this issue says the watcher
  cannot be sequenced to the interval because a hold ends before the next look. A fact with a 60 s
  half-life has to be written down at the moment it is observable, which is the next activation. Option
  three is refused on arithmetic rather than taste: the read reports the newest *completed* activation,
  and from inside a running pass that is always the pass before this one, so "once, by the next
  activation" is what the read already does for free -- a stamp file would be state able to disagree with
  the journal it is meant to dedup, and #237 already owns the residue (a repeat must read as a repeat, so
  the line carries `ended=`). Option four is refused on the issue's own recorded ground: a blind ping
  turns a hang into a silent pass, and the stalled tick is row 2 of #246's table -- still nobody's job,
  filed as its own issue rather than smuggled in beside this one. Option five is what H-0118 measured
  false: `Result=` is backwards on the polarity that matters, `timeout` on a 60 s clean-exit hold and
  `exit-code` on the 91-minute one, and `success` on all five of today's. Tie-break 1: no dependency, and
  no `require` line. Tie-break 2 not engaged -- nothing decodes -- but #228's rule is carried by hand:
  neither unknown prints a `hold=`, and a leg reddens if either one borrows the healthy number, which is
  the H-0124 bug in its second home. Tie-break 3: it refuses to print a number rather than print 0.
  Tie-break 4: three files, one function, one call site, and the manager is not asked at all -- the bus
  stays `--status`'s, where a human is the one asking, and a leg installs a `systemctl` that files a note
  the moment anything runs it, because a pass querying the unit it is running inside is the authority
  H-0118 had to disclose borrowing six times. Tie-break 5: one revertable commit, nothing published, no
  merge. What lost: two `journalctl` reads and one journal line per activation (0.01 s measured against
  this box's 400-line window), and `--status`'s sole authorship of the sentence -- the same fact is now
  composed twice from one parse, in two registers. The held line names no cause in prose deliberately:
  `deadline` is systemd's, `client` is an operator's `kill -s KILL`, `unexplained` is the journal saying
  nothing, and only the first is a descendant that ignored `SIGTERM`; the cause is `how=`, and the
  sentence that spells each one out is three lines from the same read.

## H-0130 · The queue said "the work is already written" about a branch whose whole delta against `main` is zero bytes, and the honest deliverable was a draft nobody is asked to merge

- Question: `factory/factory.sh:675` dispatched this unit as `branch_without_pr` at `issue-249` with
  the standing sentence "The work is already written. Assess it against the gate, then open its pull
  request. If the work should be dropped instead, open the pull request anyway and say so in its
  body." The assessment says the sentence's subject does not exist. The branch's one commit ahead of
  `origin/main` is `f64ddcd`, a `git commit --allow-empty` rollback checkpoint -- `git show --numstat`
  prints no file list and `git diff --stat c98f75f f64ddcd` prints nothing. The change it was cut for
  merged on 9 Nov as #252 (`mergedAt 2026-11-09T19:13:21Z`, head `c98f75f`, merge commit `93ee5f6`,
  the issue 2 seconds later in `state: CLOSED`), GitHub deleted the head ref at the merge
  (`git ls-remote origin refs/heads/issue-249` prints nothing), and after `git merge --no-edit
  origin/main` the branch's total content delta against the trunk is empty. Both endings the sentence
  offers -- deliver the work, or open a pull request that says the work should be dropped -- describe
  an object with nothing in it. What is delivered, and by which artifact?

- Options: delete the leftover local ref and record the drop in this file alone | open a ready pull
  request from the branch as it stands, a zero-byte diff offered for merge | open a **draft** pull
  request carrying this entry and no code | open nothing, comment on the ticket, and stop | escalated
  to a maintainer

- Chose: open a **draft** pull request carrying this entry and no code

- Why: option one is the exact failure the dispatch sentence was written to end -- "a branch that is
  dropped only in a local log is indistinguishable from one that was never attempted" -- and it does
  not even work as a mechanism. `factory/triage.sh:758` drops a `branch_without_pr` row exactly when
  an open pull request's `headRefName` equals the branch name; a comment, a journal line and a log
  entry are all invisible to it, so the next pass re-offers the same assessment. Only a ref deletion
  or a pull request stops the queue, and deleting a ref is the class of act this repository keeps away
  from an unattended unit (tie-break 5, the same asymmetry as
  `allow_squash_merge=false`/`allow_rebase_merge=false`) -- with a reason on this particular ref: a
  sibling `backup/issue-249-session` was cut from the same session, so the tree behind it was
  deliberately copied by a person and the copy on `main`'s side of the merge is not the only thing
  anybody wants from it. Option two asks a reviewer for a decision about nothing and, if granted,
  writes a permanent no-op merge commit into `main` for a diff that changes no file. Option four is
  what has effectively already happened twice -- the ticket is answered and the queue still dispatches
  at the branch -- because the classifier reads pull requests, not conversation. Option three is the
  only write that reaches the classifier and costs nothing the others do not also cost. It was
  verified rather than assumed at this head: `gh pr list --state open --json number,isDraft` returns
  `{"number":285,"isDraft":true}`, so a draft *is* in the list `triage.sh:124` builds with
  `gh pr list --state open --limit 100` and `:758` consults, and the row stops; and
  `triage.sh:285-286` classes a pull request marked draft as `draft` before it reaches any review arm
  while `factory/factory.sh:1162` puts `draft` in the wait arm -- so the branch becomes visible to
  every queue that reads pull requests while asking no reviewer for anything and offering the
  supervisor nothing to merge. That answers the objection to opening a pull request at all: a ready
  one would put a zero-byte diff into the review queue that `H-0116` exists to keep honest.
  Tie-break 6, the option the surrounding work already takes: `backup-tip` arrived at this same shape
  on 11 Nov in #285 -- "A disposition record, not a candidate" -- for the same reason and with the
  same reasoning, arrived at in another worktree without sight of this one.
  The branch was also given `git merge --no-edit origin/main` (187 commits) before this entry. Not to
  manufacture work: `factory/DECISIONS.md` gains at its tail and the trunk's copy carries 125 entries
  against this branch's 57, so a bare append here is a guaranteed conflict that the supervisor would
  then have to be dispatched to resolve, and a merge is the forward-only way round it (`git revert`
  still undoes everything after it; nothing is rewritten, nothing is force-pushed). The proof the
  merge carried no intent of its own is `git diff --stat origin/main..HEAD`, empty.

- Effect: this file, one entry, plus three tracker writes -- each performed and read back *before*

## H-0131 · A stranded branch is bought with a commit count, and a checkpoint commit is one commit of nothing -- so the queue paid a model to assess a zero-byte difference

- Question: `factory/triage.sh:761` (at `a0c7fce`) decides a branch is stranded work with
  `git rev-list --count "$main_sha..$sha" > 0`, and `factory/factory.sh:675` turns that number into
  the instruction "The work is already written. Assess it against the gate, then open its pull
  request." Step 3 of `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` makes every tick take a
  `git commit --allow-empty` rollback checkpoint *before* the judgement call it may never reach, so a
  tick killed by the wall-clock ceiling between the checkpoint and its effect commit leaves a ref ahead
  of `main` whose whole delta is zero bytes -- and the queue calls that work already paid for. What is
  the delivery test for a branch?
- Options: keep the count and filter the empties out of it | diff the file list from the merge base | compare patch-ids with `git cherry` | count changed bytes with `diff --shortstat` from the merge base | have a tick journal its open checkpoint and skip journalled branches | escalate
- Chose: diff the file list from the merge base
- Why: this is a measurement question, so the tie-breaks only break ties -- none of the five adds a
  dependency (#856), none touches a config default (#873), none needs a write. They separate on what
  each instrument can see, and the first is that a commit count cannot see content at all. That is the
  defect, measured at `origin/main a0c7fce`: `issue-249` at `f64ddcd` is one commit ahead,
  `git show --numstat` prints no file list, and `git diff --stat c98f75f f64ddcd` prints nothing.
  Filtering empties out of the count was the smallest edit on the list and it is wrong twice over: no
  `rev-list` flag sees an `--allow-empty` non-merge commit, which is exactly what a checkpoint is, and
  `--no-merges` removes the merge from the count -- so a branch whose only content is a conflict
  resolution would count zero and be dropped. `#291` states the same finding as "the count moves with
  the commit count and not with the content".

  `git cherry` was the strongest rival and it answers a different question. A patch-id comparison asks
  "is this change already upstream", which is the squash-and-rebase question; this repository sets
  `allow_squash_merge=false` and `allow_rebase_merge=false`, so a delivered branch's tip is an
  ancestor of `main` and the test above it (`[ "$ahead" -gt 0 ]`) already drops it. It is also
  per-commit where the deliverable is a tree: a branch that adds a file and reverts it is two non-empty
  patches and a zero-byte delta, and a pull request would carry the tree, not the patches. It loses
  because it is a sharper answer to a question this queue is not asking.

  `diff --shortstat` is the count fallacy moved one unit along: a mode change, a rename and a
  one-line semantic revert each say something about size and nothing about whether the trunk lacks the
  file. It also puts a parse in the row -- "14 files changed, 3 insertions(+)" -- where a file count is
  a command the reader can run and re-check (`git diff --name-only <base> <branch> | wc -l`).

  Journaling the open checkpoint was the only option that would also have explained *why* a branch was
  empty: a tick that wrote down "I have an un-finished checkpoint" would let the queue tell a dead tick
  from a person's abandoned probe. It loses on three counts. It is new state every other read then has
  to trust and retire; the tick that most needs it is the one the ceiling killed before it wrote; and
  `factory/factory.sh:913` records the rule this scan is built on -- "#256: everything here decides
  against refs" -- so a verdict resting on a side file is a verdict that a `git worktree prune`, or a
  second machine, silently changes. Tie-break 6 (what the surrounding code already does) is against it
  too: nothing in `triage.sh` consults a journal today.

  The merge base is not a detail; it is where this fix would have gone quietly wrong. Measured on the
  branch as `#291` found it: 0 files from the merge base (`c98f75f`, the head of the pull request that
  had already delivered it) against **21 files** from `main`'s tip, because 187 commits of other
  people's work sit between the two. Ask the content question of the tip and the empty branch is
  charged with 21 files of borrowed content and offered with a confident sentence about them. That is
  why `br-empty` in the fixture is cut before the trunk moves on and never merges it in, and why
  control 4 asks the shipped code's question of `main_sha` and requires `br-empty` back: the legs pass
  for the right reason and not for a convenient one.

  Two judgements ride with the choice. (a) A branch whose content cannot be compared -- no merge base,
  or a git that refused the diff -- keeps its row, with `content not comparable to main` printed where
  the byte count would have been and a warning naming the branch. Tie-break 3, refuse to proceed on
  missing input, in the direction #873 sets for ambiguity: dropping a person's work here is the
  irreversible side, and re-offering an empty branch costs one tick. (b) A skipped branch is not a row.
  It is a count and a name-list on stderr, printed on every pass that still sees the ref. A row is an
  offer and the ticket asks for this offer to stop; silence is what the comment at
  `factory/factory.sh:2095` "A queue that reports a thing once and" names -- and stderr is
  the channel `triage.sh` already uses for every degraded read (`:494`). A fourth class was the other
  shape of (b) and it loses because a new class needs an arm in `factory.sh` for a thing that must
  never dispatch, which is more surface around the one row that must stay inert.
- Checkpoint: c396a55d45221ba858ac358774aca40983404eb1
- Effect: `factory/triage.sh` (the branch scan: merge base, `git diff --name-only`, the skip tally and
  the unjudged tally, and the row detail as `N file(s) across M commit(s)`; the header table's branch
  row), `factory/selftest.sh` (a new section: five planted branches in a real fixture repository --
  `br-work`, `br-delete`, `br-empty`, `br-merge-empty`, `br-nobase` -- twelve legs and four control
  legs), `docs/factory.md` (the `branch_without_pr` row of the class table, and a new subsection
  "What a branch has to hold to be offered"). Measured, in the order measured: `bash
  factory/selftest.sh` **504 passed, 0 failed**, against the 488 that `H-0129` recorded at its own tip
  -- the delta is these sixteen legs. The suite's first run of these legs is part of the finding: two of
  the four controls were green while their mutant had *died* (`triage.sh:51` sources `common.sh` from
  its own directory, and the runner execs the copy directly, so a staged copy without the bit and
  without that file prints no rows at all) -- and an empty rows file makes every "this branch got no
  row" assertion true, including the control that asserts the bug came back. `branch_mutate` now stages
  both, and refuses any mutant that prints no branch row as dead rather than guilty; control 2 gained a
  positive half (`br-nobase` must stay) for the same reason. Running the shipped classifier against
  GitHub and this machine's own refs at 13:21Z on 11 Nov moved **no** row: all eight
  `branch_without_pr` rows carry content, and the file counts the new detail prints (58, 15, 14, 6, 4,
