## H-0150 · A pass stopped by the HALT marker writes no `LOG-AT`: hoist all three self-report reads above the halt block, hoist only the two read-only ones, or narrow the sentence and file the move

- Question: The review of #330 at `f282990` measured that a pass stopped by a `factory/HALT` marker leaves
  one journal line -- the `HALTED` one -- and no `LOG-AT`, while `docs/factory.md` and this harness's own
  function contract both said `LOG-AT` is "on every pass". Read back from the shipped script rather than
  quoted from the review: the halt block logs and `exit`s, `factory_body` is called later at
  `factory/factory.sh:1357`, and all four of a pass's self-report lines are inside it (`UNIT-AT` at the
  loop fed by `factory_unit_lines`, `LOG-AT` from `factory_log_move_lines`, `SUPERVISOR-AT` from
  `factory_supervisor_lines`, then `PASS`) -- so none of the four is reachable on the halt path and the
  boundary is shared by three lines, not one. It matters because the incident ask 3 was written FOR is a
  HALTED tail: the page and the pull-request body both open with `2026-11-10T10:17:21Z HALTED
  code=3962919`, and #328 measured one halt standing 10h13m. Three repairs were on the table and one
  constraint nobody had written down: the halt exit runs before `flock -n 9` at `:1292`, so hoisting moves
  `factory_log_move_lines`' copy into the journal being left -- the feature's only write outside stdout --
  outside the pass's lock, and makes an activation that loses the lock (a loser reports 7 and leaves, once
  per `FACTORY_INTERVAL`) print three lines before it goes. Which?
- Options: hoist all three read loops above the halt block, accepting the copy write and the three lines outside the lock | hoist the two read-only loops and leave `LOG-AT` inside the body, so a halted pass says the tree and the unit but not the directory | narrow the prose to "every pass that reaches the pass body", name the halt exit as the state outside the boundary, and file the move with the lock constraint for its own tick | leave the sentence and the code alone, since the review filed the finding as non-blocking
- Chose: narrow the prose to "every pass that reaches the pass body", name the halt exit as the state outside the boundary, and file the move with the lock constraint for its own tick
- Why: the tie-break that separates them is refusing rather than proceeding on an input this tick cannot
  judge. Hoisting changes what a *lock-losing* activation writes and moves an append into a file named by a
  record read off a log outside the only thing that serialises activations; this repository's own record of
  what an unguarded write to a path named by someone else's text costs is #874 and #182, and no measurement
  here says what two overlapping halted passes do to one `>>`. The option that touches no write path wins
  on that, and it also wins the next tie-break -- fewest files: three files of prose and one `local`, with
  no control flow and no leg's expectation moved, so it is reversible by `git revert` of one commit. The
  gate that decides it is the one H-0149 was raised for: a line must not state more than the code does, and
  "on every pass" beside a halt path that writes nothing is the same shape as "found no directory there"
  beside a directory that exists. Narrowing is not the same as closing, and the entry says so -- which is
  why this option carries a filed ticket (#331, with the three repairs, the lock boundary and the static
  read) rather than a silence. The fourth option is refused outright, not deferred: a page that says "every
  pass" is exactly what sends an operator to grep sibling checkouts for a tail the halt path never wrote.
  What the first option buys is real, and #331 is where the lock question gets answered; taking it here, in
  a tick dispatched because a check was red, would have spent a re-review's attention on an unlocked write
  nobody had measured.
- Consequences: `docs/factory.md` says where the boundary is and names the halt exit for `LOG-AT` and
  `SUPERVISOR-AT` alike, and `factory_log_move_lines`' contract in `factory/common.sh` says the same and
  points at #331. Two comments answer the review's findings 3 and 4: the awk `END` block now records that
  `bad` is consulted after both readable kinds, so `rc=3` is reached only when the window holds no readable
  record at all and says nothing about a damaged mark a readable record outranks, and the refusal arms carry
  the two `rc=` namespaces (the parser's 0/1/2 against the sentences' 1/2/3) with the one arm where they can
  collide named. `factory/factory.sh`'s `local` line declares `log_line`, the only loop variable it missed
  (finding 5). `docs/factory.md` records that a `--dry-run` pass performs the copy into the old journal
  (finding 2), a thing that was true and unwritten. No behaviour moves and no leg's expectation moves -- the
  gate's own wording is what follows in the pull-request body rather than here (#1180). #331 stays open

## H-0153 · The escalation step tells a tick to "label it" on a pull request and names no verb, and the verb a tick reaches for dies before gh ever reads the label name

- Question: `AGENTS.md` ends a unit that meets one of the four reserved classes by marking the artifact with the escalation label. For a pull request nothing in this harness says which command performs that mark. `factory/factory.sh:725`, the empty-ask branch of `address_review`, says "label it ${FACTORY_ESCALATION_LABEL}" and stops; `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` spells the write for an issue (`gh issue edit "$ISSUE"`) and then spells only the *read* for a pull request (`gh pr view "$PR" --json labels`), which is the shape that invites the `pr` verb for both. What has to change for the step to be followable under whichever name #311 finally chooses?
- Options: spell the working verb in the three live places that carry the step, and add a census leg | add a `factory/escalation-mark.sh` that performs the write and the read-back, so the verb has one home the way the name does | leave the instruction as prose and point the stopped unit at `docs/factory.md` for the command | escalated: the label step is #311's to settle, so touch none of it
- Chose: spell the working verb in the three live places that carry the step, and add a census leg
- Why: the step first, because a prediction about a command is not its exit status. Measured 12 Nov on this box's gh 2.46.0 at `/usr/bin/gh`, one 67-character probe name aimed at pull request #314 -- this ticket's own record PR, chosen because a refusal is its only possible outcome and it is merged, so no review state is disturbed -- with the artifact's labels read before and after and the repository's label list read before and after:

  ```
  $ gh pr edit 314 --add-label zzprobe-…-nothing-can-land
  GraphQL: Projects (classic) is being deprecated … (repository.pullRequest.projectCards)   # exit 1
  $ gh issue edit 314 --add-label zzprobe-…-nothing-can-land
  failed to update …/pull/314: 'zzprobe-…' not found
  failed to update 1 issue                                                                   # exit 1
  $ gh pr view 314 --json labels -q '[.labels[].name]|join(",")'      # before and after: empty
  $ gh label list --limit 200 --json name -q length                   # 18 before, 18 after
  ```

  Two exit 1s that do not mean the same thing, and the status is the only thing the tick sees. gh 2.46.0 reads `projectCards` on its way into `pr edit`, so that call ends **before** it resolves the label name: it cannot land a marker under any name #311 might choose, and what it prints is a sentence about Projects, not about labels, so a unit standing in that branch cannot tell "the name is still owed" from "the verb is dead". `gh issue edit` reaches the label step and names the name -- the one failure a person can actually fix. `D-0047` measured the split from the other side: `gh issue edit 240 --remove-label blocked --remove-label question` exited 0 and read back `labels: []` where `gh pr edit …` died on that field (`./DECISIONS.md:2221-2231`), and the same retired field is why Step 5 refuses `gh pr edit --add-reviewer` (H-0010). The harness had therefore already ruled this verb dead for a body and for a reviewer ask, and had never said so about the one flag whose entire job is to leave a visible mark.

  The fourth option goes first, because #311 reserves a *name* and this is not one. Nothing here chooses between `needs-human` and a label this repository has: `factory/common.sh:259` still holds the wrong word, `gh label list` still answers 18 with none of them it, and #311 stands at the end of this commit exactly where it stood at the start of it. What that ticket's own record names as owed "whatever the label ends up called" is the verb -- `H-0139`'s comment on #311, §2: "Neither option as written says which verb to name, and the sentence at `:758` needs it whatever the label ends up called" -- and #315 measured the same thing as its defect 2 and prescribed its shape ("name the working verb (`gh issue edit "$PR" --add-label …`) even when the artifact is a pull request"). Parking a fixable sentence behind an unanswerable question is the failure mode with a number on it already: #313 is the ticket that says an escalated issue is re-dispatched every activation, so every tick that concludes it may not touch #311 spends `FACTORY_TICK_TIMEOUT=2700` re-deriving the same deadlock.

  Tie-breaks, in order. 1 silent: neither option touches `go.mod`. 2 is the whole choice -- the smallest change that makes the wrong-verb outcome unreachable is to put the command where the tick is already reading, which is the instruction string in `factory/factory.sh`; a guide a tick is not required to open is not an instruction. 3: this is the step that runs when everything else has already failed, so the read-back travels in the same sentence as the write and not in a document. 4: three prose mentions and one leg, against a new script plus its legs and its shellcheck surface. 5: `git revert` reaches four edited files and would reach a new one equally well, so nothing separates the first two options here. 6 is what the first option follows: `common.sh`'s comment already declares the house pattern for this step, `escalation-label.sh` exists because "a tick in the middle of an escalation is not going to source 2,850 lines of configuration", and #272 settled that an instruction and its guide are read by different readers and both have to carry the fix.

  The second option -- `escalation-mark.sh`, the `next-decision-id.sh` pattern H-0140 just applied to the name -- was refused on what this suite can witness. A script whose body is a network write cannot be executed by these legs: the suite is offline bash and git by design, which is precisely the reason H-0140 recorded that no leg may assert the label *exists* on GitHub. So the wrapper's only test would be a text census of the wrapper -- the same witness the prose gets -- carried by a state-changing file whose happy path nothing in this repository ever runs and whose undo is a label on someone's live artifact. The third is refused for the reason the paragraph above just gave: `docs/factory.md` and the skill are read by different readers, and the tick's own prompt by neither.

  What it cost, stated plainly. **(a)** The census refuses a file that *prescribes* the dead verb -- a line that begins with it, the shape a command takes in a fenced block or a prompt string -- and deliberately does not redden on the probe quoted mid-sentence, because a leg that ate this repository's own measurements would be widened away inside a month; `esc_not_a_park` records the same objection against reddening on comment lines. A prescription written inside a sentence is therefore invisible to it, and the load-bearing half is the arm check, which reads `factory/factory.sh` as text and never runs a write. **(b)** The leg pins two whole prose phrases, one in the skill and one in the guide, so rewording either sentence reddens a leg: a leg that reads prose constrains prose, and that is #272's cure and its price in the same breath. **(c)** The tick's prompt still interpolates the name (`-- ${FACTORY_ESCALATION_LABEL} --`) while telling the tick to take the name from its one home, because `ask_prompt_assembles_it` requires that variable inside the `address_review` arm and its own failure message endorses the variable as "never spelled out"; a tick could still type the word it was shown, and deleting the interpolation to close that was refused rather than widening a measured leg this unit was not sent to widen. **(d)** No leg proves `gh issue edit` lands a *valid* label on a pull request. That is a network write, and today nobody can run it -- not a tick, not a person -- without answering #311 first, because the name the harness prints is not one of the eighteen. So the verb is verified up to gh's label-resolution step and no further, and the end-to-end escalation write stays unverified until #311 is answered. That is #311's open half, not a new hole. **(e)** #311 is not delivered by this branch. It stays open, still carrying the `blocked` stand-in its own record disclosed, and the only thing still owed on it is the decision itself.
- Checkpoint: e8db1c223158b2a1cd71843ef07b216255a47040
- Effect: `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` (step 2 names the verb a pull request takes; the measurement is the paragraph *after* the code block, beside the probe measurement already there -- a second `gh issue edit … --add-label` line inside the block would break `esc_step_control`'s plant, which requires exactly one); `factory/factory.sh` (the empty-ask branch carries the two calls, with the command substitution escaped so the tick runs it in its own worktree rather than the supervisor expanding it at prompt-build time); `docs/factory.md` (the verb paragraph in "What an escalation leaves on the artifact"); `factory/selftest.sh` (`esc_pr_verb`, plus `esc_pr_verb_control` with three plants -- the dead verb restored as a command line, the two commands lifted out of the instruction, the guide sentence deleted -- each checked to have landed before it is asserted). Measured: `claim_leg` calls 285 → 286; `bash factory/selftest.sh` **564 passed, 0 failed**, all three controls reported; `grep -rn` over `scripts/mutations/*.json` for `factory/factory.sh` and `factory/selftest.sh` answers nothing, so `make check-mutations` was not run for this commit; `make verify` → `verify: OK`, exit 0, run once across the four changed files without this entry and once more with this entry in the tree, both results quoted in the pull-request body (#1180: an `Effect:` written before the gate runs is a prophecy).

## H-0154 · The tally sentence #291 asked for printed its own format string, and the repair that lasts refuses the shape rather than fixing two lines

- Question: `#329` reads `factory/triage.sh` off `origin/main` = `f5e0fe9` and quotes what it puts on
  stderr. Reproduced here with the file's own bytes -- `sed -n` of the two lines into a script that sets
  the two counters, no hand-retyped copy anywhere in the path -- on bash 5.3.9, with three content-free
  branches: 277 bytes of stderr and not one newline in them.

  ```
  triage: offered: %s\n branch(es) ahead of main hold no content the trunk lacks, so none is
  triage: 3 branch(es) ahead of main hold no content the trunk lacks, so none is
  triage: issue-302 issue-309 issue-318 branch(es) ahead of main … so none is
  ```

  The literal is closed and the backslash follows with nothing between them, so the shell deletes
  `\<newline>` and what remains between the two literals is the continuation line's own indentation: a
  field separator. `printf` is therefore handed a format with one slot and no `\n`, plus the literal
  `offered: %s\n` as its first argument, and POSIX printf re-applies the format while arguments remain.
  Both sites in the file are this shape. The ticket offers two repairs and the second one changes what
  `make verify` refuses, which is a rule written against every unit that comes after -- so: repair the
  two format strings, teach `scripts/check-scripts.py` the shape, do both, or hand it up?
- Options: repair the two format strings and stop, since stderr is not the machine-readable half and the rows are built by `emit` elsewhere | teach `scripts/check-scripts.py` to refuse the shape and leave the sentences as shipped, on the theory that a red gate will force the edit sooner than a person will | repair both sites, teach the guard the shape, and pin both polarities in the guard's own self-test so it can be neither ignored nor widened away | escalate, because a new gate rule binds every unit and is not a unit's call
- Chose: repair both sites, teach the guard the shape, and pin both polarities in the guard's own self-test so it can be neither ignored nor widened away
- Why: three measurements decided the shape of the repair, and the first is why "stop at the strings"
  loses. `bash -n` exits 0 and `shellcheck -S style` exits 0 on the broken file -- the parse is legal and
  the tooling that `verify` already runs is blind to it, so nothing stops the next person writing the
  same continuation; this is the second line-continuation defect in this one file (the first, caught
  while H-0131 was in review, was a `\<newline>` placed *inside* the quotes, which the shell keeps
  literal). The second measurement is why the existing legs did not catch it either: the two needles
  that guard this sentence, `hold no content the trunk lacks` and `br-empty br-merge-empty`, both
  `grep -qF` clean against the mangled stderr, because the format's own words are precisely what got
  printed. A leg that matches a fragment of a sentence is not an assertion about that sentence, so the
  legs now assert each sentence whole and assert that no literal `%s` or `\n` reaches stderr at all. The
  third is why a gate rule must ship in the same commit as the fix: a rule that reddens the tree it
  arrives in is a rule that gets reverted, and repairing both sites is what lets the rule land green on
  day one. Both *correct* shapes are pinned in the guard's accepted set -- the house idiom
  `printf '…%s\n' \` (a space between quote and backslash, so the arguments are what continues) and the
  column-0 join, which really does concatenate -- because the flag guard's own history says what happens
  otherwise: its first draft refused six working call sites and had to be narrowed (#217). Control 5
  asks the shipped shape of the repaired file and demands the sentence come back broken, with the
  dead-mutant floor this section already documents, so the control cannot pass by failing to start.
  The rule then proved itself in the field rather than in a fixture: while testing it,
  `git checkout -- factory/triage.sh` restored the checkpoint commit, which does not contain the
  repair, and two lines later `check-scripts` refused `factory/triage.sh:1019` and `:1023` again on a
  tree that looked clean in `git status`. What is *not* claimed here: that the third leg's needle
  (`no merge base with main`) also survives its sentence's mangling. The probe that measured the other
  two ran with `unjudged_count=0`, so that sentence never printed and its needle went missing for a
  reason that has nothing to do with the bug.
- Checkpoint: d2d8eedf8346e263f389a2acde6b9b033778aaca
- Effect: factory/triage.sh, factory/selftest.sh, scripts/check-scripts.py, docs/factory.md


## H-0155 · An escalation's label was the one half of its ending no pass could read, so an honest unit burned a fresh ceiling

- Question: Where does a unit's stop become visible, when it is told to comment, label and stop and only the comment is read?

- Options: read nothing and trust a person to reopen the issue when the queue offers the same ticket for the fourth time | class the marker in `factory/triage.sh` and emit a `parked` row the supervisor logs and never dispatches, `delivered` still winning the row | a ledger file beside the queue state carrying the same fact, keyed by issue number | let the marker choose any class, so a unit can also mark its own work delivered or claim the next assignment

- Chose: class the marker in `factory/triage.sh` and emit a `parked` row the supervisor logs and never dispatches, `delivered` still winning the row

- Escalated: no

- Refers: H-0140

- Why: Tie-break 3 (safety over liveness) chose the class and also decided its shape. The measured cost of the silence is one ticket eating the queue: `#301` went out at 20:11, 21:07 and 22:03Z on 13 Nov and each pass ended `TICK-FAILED … exit=124 (124 means the 2700s ceiling)`, its `updatedAt` unmoved since the previous day because the terminal write is the first thing a truncated budget costs, while `#284` -- open, claimed by nothing -- never reached a tick at all behind it. The mechanism is `65e980b`'s `FACTORY_CLAIM_STALE_FAILS=3`: an open body naming its own issue is one of the two claim channels, so an escalation that ships no pull request re-claims its own ticket and is re-offered; and `grep -c labels` answered `0` for `triage.sh` and `0` for `factory.sh` there and again at `f5e0fe9`, so the half of the ending a machine could see had never existed. Tie-break 6 (convention) wrote it: the row is emitted at the `unclaimed` emit site with `delivered` ahead of it, in the same TSV, and consumed by a `park)` arm shaped exactly like `delivered)` -- one `log_event`, no tick -- because the tick would be sent to make the decision the unit refused to make, and the name is read through `factory/escalation-label.sh` for the reason H-0140 gives. Tie-break 4 (reversibility) settled the rest: nothing is written to the platform, one row and six stderr sentences, all of it a `git revert`. The second option over the third because `triage.sh`'s own header refuses a second source of the same claim -- a ledger beside the queue would be "the same claim with a filename on it" -- and the queue payload is already fetched with the issues it classes. What lost, and it is not small: H-0140's `esc_not_a_park` pinned that the marker has **no vote in the queue**, and this narrows it. The surviving invariant is the direction, so the leg became a window scan -- a label-bearing line in `triage.sh`, and the two after it, may name `parked` and no other class -- which keeps the thing the pin was really for: a unit's own marker may stop a dispatch, and may neither pick the class a tick is dispatched on nor grade its own work as delivered. #311 still owns the name itself: `gh label list` measured 18 names on 12 Nov with none of them the instructed one, so until that is answered the classifier parks nothing and says which name it looked for on every pass, which is a reported refusal rather than the silence of the third option. `labels(first:10)` is a bound that fails one way only -- a match at the tenth label is still a match -- so the warning names just the issues that filled the list without matching, which stay workable rather than being called parked. Measured: `bash factory/selftest.sh` **589 passed, 0 failed**; the block adds 28 `claim_leg` calls and retires one, a net of 27, and controls add legs to nothing.

- Checkpoint: b934f384b8b174d4cf8769a0f176a176d91089b2

- Effect: `factory/triage.sh` (the issue query carries `labels(first:10) { nodes { name } }`; one `gh label list --limit 200 --json name` read per pass, its absence and its failures told apart; `park_json`, `park_field` and `park_bound` derived by jq from the payload the pass already fetched; `park_json` beside `reopen_json`; the emit at the `unclaimed` site; six stderr sentences -- no `labels` field on any issue, the issues that filled `labels(first:10)`, an unreadable label list, a list that was not a list, a label read stopped at its 200-name bound, and the name absent from the repository); `factory/factory.sh` (the `park)` arm, 1 case); `factory/selftest.sh` (the `label list` shim arm with its fail and garbage answers, `claim_park_on` / `claim_park_many` / `claim_park_without` plants, 27 net legs, `esc_not_a_park` narrowed to the window scan and its control reworded, every plant deriving the name rather than spelling it); `factory/common.sh` (the constant's comment, which claimed the marker was not an input to the queue); `docs/factory.md` (the class table's `parked` row and the paragraph naming the measured ticks). The fixture's own defect found by this work: a leg that removed the name from `label list` while leaving it on the issue printed no absent-label sentence at all, because the marker is matched on the issue's labels and the repository list is only ever a courtesy to the reader -- the leg was wrong, the classifier was right, and both polarities are pinned now.

## H-0156 · A merged body's closing keyword is a request to GitHub and nothing ever asked whether it was granted, so the loop now reads the issue back — and reads the body span-blind, because the tidier scan cannot see the defect

- Question: after `gh pr merge` succeeds, the issues the body named with `Closes #N` are never read back. Measured over all 176 merged pull requests here, a keyword in plain text closed its issue within two seconds of the merge 92 times in 94 — with nothing at all in the three-to-120-second bucket — while a keyword inside inline code closed 0 in 2: #308's `` `Closes #304` `` left #304 to a hand close 6086 s later, and #338's `` `Closes #301.` `` sat on a line stating the keyword was deliberate and left #301 open 14472 s past the merge, which is what cost a second unit on a ticket trunk had already delivered. What does the loop do when the keyword did not do what the body said it did?
- Options: close the issue and comment, since the body asked for it | comment and journal only, and leave the state change to a person | halt the activation until the ticket is resolved | write nothing and let `triage.sh` notice on a later pass
- Chose: comment and journal only, and leave the state change to a person
- Why: three measurements decided this, and one of them argues against the option that looks strongest. **The re-probe exists because GitHub's closer is asynchronous.** A single read milliseconds after a merge is not an answer, so the check sleeps `FACTORY_CLOSE_PROBE` (10 s default — five times the widest delta in the measured population) and reads again; 10 s buys one read on the rare ticket rather than a false note on every slow one. **The window is stated, not tuned.** `FACTORY_CLOSE_FIRED_S` defaults to 120 because the population has zero pairs between 3 and 120 s, so any bound from 3 s to 27000 s separates the same two sets; the two plain-text outliers are +27586 s and +159415 s, and the two code-span ones +6086 s and +14472 s. **Closing is refused because a merge is not evidence about requirements.** #1256 is this repository's record of a keyword firing on a line written to *negate* it, and #301 is the case where a body named two issues and the right answer was to refuse to close either — a component that closes on the strength of a verb would have made that call with less information than the unit had. Halting is refused for the reason #341 documents: one un-closed ticket must not park every later activation. Writing nothing is the status quo that cost the unit. **The scan is span-blind on purpose:** stripping code spans first models GitHub faithfully and would have reported no claim for #301 at all, because the specimen IS a keyword inside a span; the check has to read the body the way `CLAIM_RE` does — which takes a backtick as filler — and then compare against what GitHub reports, so the disagreement is the finding. The note quotes the verb lines inside a code span of its own, which is load-bearing twice: it shows the reader which case they are looking at, and a note that put `Closes #301` in running text would close the very ticket it is reporting on. `scripts/check-close-verb.py` reads the generated note and reports `inert #301`, nothing firing — pinned by a leg. The healthy path writes no journal line at all (#334 priced a pass at 37 lines already), and a failure to read is never reported as an open ticket: unreadable issue is `CLOSE-CHECK-UNKNOWN`, unreadable body is `CLOSE-CHECK-SKIPPED`, no timestamp is `CLOSE-UNTIMED`.
- Checkpoint: 022bb7876885036c957b99e93ccfb53293ff8f63
- Effect: `factory/factory.sh` (`factory_verify_closure` and `factory_close_delta`, called from `factory_merge` after the merged-at stamp), `scripts/check-close-verb.py` (new, with `--self-test`), `Makefile` (the contract line in `verify`), `factory/selftest.sh` (a section that sources the shipped bytes over three stubs, plus a control that empties the function), `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` (Step 5, where every example was a code span), `docs/factory.md` (the population table and the span-blind reasoning)
- Refers: #353 (this ticket), #301/#338 and #304/#308 (the two specimens, and the re-dispatch #301 cost), #341 (a halt is not the answer to one bad ticket), #334 (the journal's size), #1256 (the parser has no notion of negation — the reason the note quotes inside a span), #1180 (read the artifact back; a write's exit status is not its effect — the same error aimed at a verb instead of a call), #1264 (this repository offers only a merge commit, so what merges is permanent)

## H-0157 · A ref with no pull request is refused by its name and by its bytes, and neither judgement is allowed to invent a class

- Question: A branch ahead of `main` with no open pull request is offered to a tick as stranded work.
  Some of those refs are kept copies, some are work already sitting in an open pull request, and some
  are contributions. Who decides, on what evidence, and what does the queue do with the answer -- a new
  class, or something the supervisor already refuses?
- Options: A name test only, widened to the families the refs actually use | A content test only,
  comparing every ref against every open pull request head | Both -- the name test refuses the family
  names and `triage.sh` marks a ref whose bytes are already on an open pull request head, the mark
  riding in the `branch_without_pr` detail for the supervisor arm to refuse on | A new row class for a
  ref delivered by an open pull request, beside the delivered row #291 shipped
- Chose: Both -- the name test refuses the family names and `triage.sh` marks a ref whose bytes are
  already on an open pull request head, the mark riding in the `branch_without_pr` detail for the
  supervisor arm to refuse on
- Why: The name alone cannot settle whether a ref was delivered. `backup-tip` was 7 files and 5 commits
  ahead of `main` and `preserve/issue-318-wip` 6 across 3, both printed as workable rows at 00:38Z on
  14 Nov, while `wip/issue-220-refused-frames` carried content and is still not
  something to point a session at -- the two questions are independent, so option 1 and option 2 each
  answer one of them. The content test lives in `triage.sh` because that is where the open payload is
  already paid for; #277 measured that read at 43 s against a 10 s all-up queue, and H-0013 prices a
  network read in front of a dispatch at 5min2s, so `factory.sh` may not ask again. Option 4 re-invents
  what #291 shipped and does it the dangerous way, because a class retires a ref. The reading is bytes,
  and the measurement that decided it is why `git cherry` is not in the file: it marks a commit `-`
  when the commit is **empty**, not when the work landed. Measured at 00:50Z on 14 Nov, `issue-248`,
  `issue-309` and `issue-318` are each one empty commit with zero files and all three read
  patch-equal to every non-draft open head -- a verdict about the shape of a commit, never about
  whether work landed. What replaced it is
  the head itself when the ref is contained in it, otherwise one `git diff` between the two trees
  restricted to the files the ref touches. The merge-base form was written first and discarded: a change
  cherry-picked onto the pull request head still names the file in a merge-base diff, which is the only
  case the reading exists for. A draft head buys no refusal: a draft never merges, so a match against
  it retires work no delivery will ever cover. The shape is draft #285 on `backup-tip` ("reference
  only, do not merge", closed unmerged at 16:34:58Z on 12 Nov), not a live instance of it.
  What lost: `preserve-scroll-position` and `tmp-dir-cleanup` are now refused, because a family word is
  also the first token of a feature branch, and bare `backup` is still not refused, because `[-/]` asks
  for a family or a path and not for the word.
- Consequences: The arm in `factory/factory.sh` refuses on the mark's first characters the way the
  `delivered` arm reads `[merged-pr:`, because the detail is prose and carries somebody else's branch
  name; the pull request number in the journal is cut off the front of the detail rather than
  re-derived from git, so it names the pull request the classifier actually looked at. Two named bounds,
  `FACTORY_DELIVERED_WINDOW` and `FACTORY_DUP_SCAN` (40, against the 5 open heads measured 23:20Z on
  13 Nov), and past either one the row says `[dup-scan-limited:N …]` and draws no conclusion rather than
  a cheap one. The ticket's 12 Nov premise that the arm refuses nothing is recorded false -- 24
  `REFUSED branch` lines, 11 Nov 09:54:49Z through 14:14:10Z. The content refusal fires on no live ref:
  the shipped classifier against the real queue at 00:45Z on 14 Nov prints 11 `branch_without_pr` rows
  and 37 `branch delivered`, with no mark and no bound note, so that half is pinned by the fixture
  alone, and what the name half
  changes live is three refs -- `backup-tip`, `preserve/issue-222-stale-base`, `preserve/issue-318-wip`
  -- which keep their rows and lose their tick.
- Checkpoint: 3c2d68fbf16215b61145261698097718a1b6b6d3
- Effect: `factory/common.sh` (`FACTORY_DELIVERED_WINDOW`, `FACTORY_DUP_SCAN`, `FACTORY_DUP_MARK`),
  `factory/factory.sh` (`factory_refuseto_work` widened to `[-/]` per family, with the `preserve`

## H-0158 -- A zero-byte file named after a verdict that was never reached

- Question: every tick that GETS its worktree leaves a zero-byte `factory/run/worktree-error.<pid>` behind,
  because only the failure arm deletes the file. Is that file a verdict that has to be earned, or is the
  age-bound sweep the thing to tune?
- Options: Keep the name `worktree-error.<pid>` and delete the file on both paths | Name the stream for what it is while it is only a stream -- `worktree-stderr.<pid>` -- delete it on both paths, and let the sweep match the retired name beside the new one | Take the file away and have `factory_worktree` journal its own reason before returning, so nothing in the run directory needs deleting | Tune the sweep's age bound, the repair the file's own comment recommended for eight days
- Chose: Name the stream for what it is while it is only a stream -- `worktree-stderr.<pid>` -- delete it on both paths, and let the sweep match the retired name beside the new one
- Why: the name is the defect. Measured at 00:54Z on 14 Nov -- four markers in `factory/run/`
  (`worktree-error.{3101739,3420682,4010611,747393}`, all 0 bytes, stamped 22:03, 22:59, 23:31 and 00:22Z,
  the last four ticks), and `grep -c 'no worktree' factory/log/supervisor.log` answers **0**: the failure the
  name reports has never once been journaled on this machine. Three reads of that directory on two days each
  concluded from those files that the supervisor cannot build trees at all and the queue is stalled; the
  first two changed what was reported about live queue state. The last option is what the wrong reason
  produced, and bounding by age is precisely what leaves three hours of alarms standing in the directory at
  all times. The first removes this incident and keeps the false sentence for the next reader who finds a
  marker under the bound. The third is the largest change to the refusal sentence -- the reason has to reach
  the journal line, because a terminal reader and a journalled reader see different amounts
  (`factory/factory.sh:765-771`), and the file exists at all because folding stderr into the command
  substitution splices an error sentence into the value assigned to `tree` (`:773-776`).
- Invariant maintained: the refusal's reason still reaches the journal line -- a leg requires the stream's own
  words (`checked out in`) inside `TICK-SKIPPED … no worktree for issue-900 ::`, and another forbids the
  fallback sentence `common.sh gave no reason`, which is what an unread or empty stream produces. A killed
  tick's stream is still swept, and a marker inside the bound is still spared for a supervisor running right
  now. Both polarities are legs, not prose.
- What lost: the success path does a delete that is not needed for correctness -- it is there for the reader,
  and a control pins it rather than a sentence trusting it. The `find` is one line, which gives up the
  wrapped readability so a control can replace the command whole instead of retyping tabs and backslashes (a
  mistyped mutant is a dead mutant, not a guilty one). `worktree-error.` survives only as a sweep term, so
  anything that counted it now counts nothing new; the only readers in-tree were `factory/factory.sh` itself
  and this log.
- Effect: `factory/factory.sh` (the stream name, the success-path delete, the sweep's two names, and the
  comment whose "eight zero-byte files in a day" claimed eight killed ticks when the run directory held four
  and the failure sentence had never been written); `factory/selftest.sh` (the new section -- eleven
  `proc_leg` calls, two of them controls, plus `proc_mutate_last`, because the neighbouring
  `proc_mutate_factory` refuses an anchor that does not occur exactly once and both arms of this `if` carry
  the same `rm -f` sentence); `docs/factory.md` (the run directory as a reader meets it).
- Checkpoint: 874d9a4ddc9bbbb5012e8f3a0957e15cf52fd6c3
- Refs: #351, #216 (where the wrong reason entered), #228, H-0044 (the verdict has to be sayable in the
  journal line)
- Follow-up: none. Ask 3 of #351 -- correct the comment instead of letting the sweep stay the repair -- is in
  the same commit as the sentence it corrects.

## H-0160 · The blank-byte check in `factory_stop_reason` expands the whole tick log inside bash, so *where* a multibyte character sits decides how long a finished tick takes -- 163 s on a real 441 KB log, in an arm no ceiling in this harness bounds

- Id: this entered the harness log as `H-0154` on `issue-344`, and that number is published on `main` as *The tally sentence #291 asked for printed its own format string, and the repair that lasts refuses the shape rather than fixing two lines* -- written in `3f3f459`, merged as PR #350 on `issue-329` at 2026-11-13T20:56:44-05:00. A merged entry's id never moves, so the unmerged side yields, which is `docs/factory.md`'s rule and not a preference: moving `main`'s would be a force-push against history the only merge this repository offers makes permanent. The two decisions that held 154 share nothing but the digit: that one is a `printf` format continued onto an indent, this one a bash expansion priced by where its multibyte characters fell. What the yield cannot move: `d9465d6` keeps `Decision: H-0154` in its message and is not rewritten -- a rewrite is a force-push here -- so `git log --grep='Decision: H-0160'` finds this rename and not the work, and `git log --grep='Decision: H-0154'` now arrives at the tally sentence for a change that measures a multibyte expansion. The mapping lives in this line alone. Nothing else on this branch named the number, so no citation had to be chased: `grep -rn 'H-0154'` over the merged tree returns three lines, all of them main's (its own heading, the `check-scripts.py` sentence in `docs/factory.md`, and the comment above the repaired `printf` in `factory/triage.sh`), and nothing belonging to `issue-344`. No `path:NNN` citation is written here for that reason -- `#318` is the record of what one costs. The `Checkpoint:` below still names `a6895403`, the rollback target of the edit itself; the checkpoint for this merge is `8cf99b8`, and `git revert -m 1` on the merge commit is what undoes the renumbering.
- Question: `factory_stop_reason` has to know whether a tick log holds one non-blank byte before it says anything about why the session stopped, because a log of nothing but newlines is a non-empty string and every reader downstream would be handed a blank as if it were content. The shipped version asked that of a single bash expansion, `[ -z "${clean//[[:space:]]/}" ]`, over the whole log. What is the repair, given that the verdict must stay byte-for-byte the same, and that the call sits where no timeout can reach it?
- Options: stream the test to a forked `grep -q` fed by a here-string | stream it through a pipe, `printf '%s\n' "$clean" | grep -q '[^[:space:]]'` | stream it from `tr` through a process substitution so no value is built for this test | keep the test in bash and replace `[[:space:]]` with an ASCII bracket set | keep the expansion and test only a bounded prefix of the value | leave the expansion and bound the cleanup arm with `timeout`
- Chose: stream the test to a forked `grep -q` fed by a here-string
- Why: the shape is the cost, and the cost is not linear in the size. A whole-value parameter substitution re-synchronises its multibyte decode from byte 0 for every multibyte character in the value, so what it costs is multibyte characters multiplied by how far into the value they sit. Measured on the harness's own `20261104T153010Z.unclaimed:202.log` -- 441,215 bytes carrying 487 of them, every one ordinary prose (EM DASH, MIDDLE DOT, arrows; 1,269 non-ASCII bytes, zero invalid) -- the expansion took **162.88 s and 164.43 s** on a quiet 32-cpu box and the streamed test **0.01 s**, three passes each. The body of #344 had said 171.793 s; that pass ran under load, and the addendum corrects it to the quiet figure.
  - Placement, not count, is the driver: two synthetic files of that same size with that same 487 characters cost **207.96 s scattered and 9.29 s clustered** at byte 1000. An ASCII-only projection of the same 441 KB -- same size, no multibyte at all -- still took **6.914 s**, so the expansion is already expensive and scatter multiplies it. That last number is what refutes the fourth option: replacing the class with an ASCII bracket set `[ $'\t' $'\n' $'\v' $'\r' $'\f' ]` measured **263.11 s** on the same file (that one under load, and the load cannot explain three orders of magnitude). It is the whole-value substitution that is wrong, whatever is inside its brackets.
  - Blast radius, both corpora: over the 218 archived logs, 44 needed more than the 25 s a probe was willing to wait and 14 more needed over a second -- 27 %. Over the 114 logs in the directory the timer actually writes, `/home/rodney/prj/parental-lockout/factory/log`, **60 exceeded 25 s and 98 (86 %) exceeded one second**, so the median live log is already in the band; logs written the day this was measured include a 641,708-byte one past the bound and a 193 KB one at 23.886 s.
  - Why this arm and not a slow-but-harmless one: the marker call is `d9465d6:factory/factory.sh:876`, inside `factory_tick` (:632) in the **supervisor's own shell**. The `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=60 "$FACTORY_TICK_TIMEOUT"` at `d9465d6:factory/factory.sh:809` bounds the `opencode run` child and nothing after it, so by the time this expansion runs the 2700 s ceiling is already spent. Nothing else covers it either: the pass budget is "spent before opening a tick, never during one" (`d9465d6:factory/factory.sh:1040-1043`) and the whole activation runs under `flock -n 9` (`d9465d6:factory/factory.sh:1302`), so a stall here is not one unit waiting, it is the queue waiting, and a stray-process reaper cannot help because the slow process is the supervisor itself.
  - Why a here-string rather than the pipe: this file's entry points all run `set -euo pipefail` (`factory/factory.sh:42` "set -euo pipefail", declared at `common.sh:4` "Sourced, never executed."), and `grep -q` exits at its first match, so a `printf` still writing 441 KB into that pipe can die of `SIGPIPE` and answer for a pipeline that had already found its byte. A here-string leaves one command in the pipeline position and its status is `grep`'s alone. Both were measured, not assumed: on content-early, content-only-at-the-end and whitespace-only fixtures, with `pipefail` on, the pipe gave rc 0/0/1, the here-string 0/0/1, and the shipped expansion 1/1/0 -- equivalent verdicts, and the cost difference between them is zero (0.01 s either way, 0.00 s for the process-substitution form).
  - What lost. The third option is the fastest of the four sound ones (0.00 s) and went second to last: not building `$clean` for this test is a real saving, but `$clean` is what the rest of the function already reads, so the choice would have been between two variables holding the same 441 KB or a `tr` run twice per tick, to save nothing measurable. The fifth is not slow, it is **unsound** -- a log that opens with 200 KB of blanks and ends in prose would be reported as a session that wrote nothing at all, which is a different defect with the same journal line. The sixth trades a correct verdict for a wrong one at the same cost: a `timeout` on the arm turns 163 s into "the stop reason is unknown" *and* still spends the seconds. And every option here pays one fork (~7 ms) against the forks this function already makes -- `tr` plus the existing tail read is 0.01 s on the same file -- which is the price of a verdict that does not depend on where the dashes fell.
  - Tie-breaks, in order. 1 silent: nothing here touches `go.mod`; `check-deps` says `stdlib only`. 2 is the whole choice: one line replaced, and the wrong outcome becomes unreachable rather than merely bounded. 3: the verdict is the contract of this function, so the option that keeps it byte-for-byte wins over the one that answers faster and differently. 4: a fork per tick against a queue-stopping stall. 5: `git revert` reaches one line and one section. 6 is what the chosen option follows: the file already streams its other reads through `grep` and `awk`, so this is the house shape, not a new one.
- Checkpoint: a6895403e255450fdb2189f5ad55d65da46d001a
- Effect as shipped by #352: `factory/common.sh` (the blank test at the head of `factory_stop_reason`, with the measurement above it, including why the here-string and not the pipe); `factory/selftest.sh` (`$stop_dir/dense.log` -- 1,300 lines at four EM DASHes per 94-character line, 137,835 bytes, 1,301 lines, 5,200 multibyte characters -- `stop_leg 'a dense log is read, not mulled over'` for the verdict, and `dash_ctl`, which bounds the real sourced function and the replaced expression under the same `timeout 1`). Measured: the fixture costs 14.66 s the old way and 0.01 s the new way, so the 1 s bound carries 14x of margin against the regression and 100x against a loaded box; `bash factory/selftest.sh` **564 passed, 0 failed** before and **566 passed, 0 failed** after, with the control printing `function rc=1, old shape rc=124`; the leg bites -- a copy of `common.sh` outside the repository with the substitution restored answers the fixture at **rc=124** under that bound while the tree answers **rc=1**, and the tracked file was never touched; `make check-shell` → `check-shell: 0.10.0 over 29 scripts`, exit 0; `make verify` → `verify: OK`, exit 0, its own tally line reading `selftest.sh: 566 passed, 0 failed`; `grep -rl factory scripts/mutations/` answers nothing, so the mutation corpus (Go packages only) has no set over these files and `make check-mutations` was not run. The second `make verify`, with this entry in the tree, answered `verify: OK`, exit 0, its own log reading `check-decisions: 207 entries`, `selftest.sh: 566 passed, 0 failed` and `check-deps: stdlib only` -- both runs quoted in the pull-request body (#1180: an `Effect:` written before the gate runs is a prophecy). ## H-0164 · #357's review blocks on the width of one pattern: a 20-character filler window invents 15 closers GitHub was never asked for, two of the stems are not GitHub's keywords, and the copy that invented them is asymmetric

- Question: `gh pr view 357 --json headRefName,updatedAt` (the type read of #2027 -- a bare
  `--json number` answers the same for an issue) says `issue-353`, and the review submitted at
  `2026-11-14T05:13:30Z` is `CHANGES_REQUESTED` against head `f27b614`, so it was written after the 17
  commits of `main` and before this branch's resolution of them. Its blocking 1 is "the 20-character
  filler window claims closers GitHub was never asked for"; its blocking 2 is "two of the stems are not
  GitHub's keywords"; and it says plainly that none of its four blocking items touches the design. The
  population was re-derived here rather than inherited: `gh pr list --state merged --limit 1000
  --json number,body,mergedAt` -> 180 rows, `gh issue list --state all --limit 1000 --json
  number,state,closedAt` -> 175 rows, both re-run minutes before the counts below, and
  `/tmp/opencode/p357/audit_closers.py` IMPORTS `CLOSER` out of `scripts/check-close-verb.py` instead of
  re-typing it, so the count and the shipped rule cannot disagree by transcription. Shipped pattern: 100
  plain-text pairs naming an issue, 98 closed within 2 s of their merge, 2 late (#207 +159415 s, #211
  +27586 s) and zero in the 3-to-120 s band; 2 inline-code-only pairs, 0 fired (#304 +6086 s, #301
  +14472 s); 0 fenced. `CLOSER_RE` as it stood at the checkpoint below -- `clos(?:e|es|ed|ing)
  |fix(?:e[sd])?|resolv(?:e|es|ed|ing)` then `\b[^#\n]{0,20}` -- answers 107 plain-text pairs plus 8
  naming a pull request or nothing: 115 matches where 100 exist, 15 of them invented. What the pattern
  is FOR decides whether 15 inventions are free: `factory_verify_closure` writes its verdict as a
  comment on the named ticket, so an invented closer is a false sentence on a live artifact. How wide
  may a closer be, do the `-ing` stems stay, is `\s` a legal separator, and does one spelling become the
  source of the other?
- Options: keep the shipped window and the `-ing` stems, because they are the shape `triage.sh`'s claim
  matcher already uses and the harness should notice anything a person might have meant | GitHub's
  documented keyword set, adjacent (`[:, \t]*`), in both shipped spellings, with a leg pinning the two
  engines against each other | the window kept in `factory.sh` so the span-blind scan keeps seeing
  intent, narrowed only in the checker | narrowed in `factory.sh` and the checker left wide | `\s*` as
  the separator, so a tab, a newline or a `\r` all count | one spelling imported from the other (the
  checker parses `CLOSER_RE` out of `factory.sh`, or `factory.sh` shells into the checker) so they
  cannot drift | separate the two jobs honestly: keep the claim matcher wide, narrow only the closer,
  and write down that they are different questions | ship the audit script in the branch so the
  population is re-derivable by anyone with `gh` access
- Chose: GitHub's documented keyword set, adjacent (`[:, \t]*`), in both shipped spellings, with a leg
  pinning the two engines against each other
- Why: a closer is not a claim, and the two widths answer different questions. The claim matcher's job is
  "did anybody say anything about this ticket", where a backtick and a long sentence are both worth
  noticing, and H-0156 makes this scan span-blind for exactly that reason. The closer's job is "what did
  GitHub agree to do", and GitHub's list is nine words -- close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed,
  resolve, resolves, resolved -- with the reference touching the verb. Option 1 is the measured defect:
  15 invented pairs, 7 naming real issues no sentence asked about. The most expensive is live now --
  `pull request #292 has the fix. Refs #291 for context only.`, merged in #293, read by the window as a
  request for #291, which is still OPEN, so the function would comment on #291 that its own merge failed
  to close it, about a keyword never aimed at it; another invented pair names #228, closed 29398 s BEFORE
  the merge that "closed" it. Options 3 and 4 are refused by the pairing: the checker is what a unit runs
  on its own body before it opens the pull request, so a checker that still sees a window tells the
  author a closer exists where GitHub sees none, and the guard argues with itself. Option 5 is a window
  by another name, refused by the shape of every scan here -- `jq` gets `splits("\n")`, the checker
  iterates `splitlines()` -- so a separator that can match a newline never pays off inside one line and
  can only ever match a `\r` out of a CRLF body; measured, `[:,\s]*` and `[:, \t]*` give the identical
  population today, which is why the narrow one is free. Option 6 was the tempting one and fails
  mechanically: the two engines are different dialects handed to different programs (Oniguruma to `jq`,
  `re` to Python), so importing means one program parsing the other's escaping, and a leg costs less
  than that parser. Option 7 is where the `-ing` forms belong -- kept in `CLAIM_RE`, dropped here -- and
  the checkpoint's line is the evidence of what hand-copying a stem list does: `clos...|ing` and
  `resolv...|ing` came across and `fix(?:e[sd])?` has no `-ing` arm, so one merged body's spelling

  Option 8 is right in principle and wrong in this commit: the audit reads `gh` dumps and `/tmp`, so it

## H-0165 · #357's review asks which number a verb actually pointed at: `capture` reports the first on the line, and the re-probe arm had its own copy of the verdict with only the healthy branch in it

- Question: the same `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review as H-0164, against the same head `f27b614`, filed four
  more items beside the pattern ones -- blocking 3, and non-blocking 1, 2 and 6 -- and all four are about
  the pass that reads GitHub's answer rather than the rule that reads the body. Blocking 3 is that `jq`
  was asked for a `capture`, which answers the FIRST `#N` on a matching line and nothing else, so "a line
  with two references reports the wrong one and misses the right one, and `Closes #1 and Closes #2`
  reports only #1". Non-blocking 1 is that the re-probe arm decided for itself and printed a healthy
  sentence for an untimed close and for a 40400 s close. Non-blocking 6 is the sleep inside the loop.
  Non-blocking 2 is that five of the function's arms had no leg. Each was reproduced before it was
  believed: `printf '%s\n' '#7 is the reason. Fixes #12.' | jq -Rsr '[splits("\n") | select(test($re)) |
  capture("#(?<n>[1-9][0-9]*)").n]'` answers `["7"]` and the same body through `scan($re)` answers `12`;
  `Closes #301 and Closes #304.` answers `301` alone. For the re-probe arm, the fixture run over the bytes
  at `8c9999b` printed `CLOSE-SETTLED pr:1 issue:2 closed unknown s after the merge, inside the window
  GitHub takes` for a ticket that went OPEN then CLOSED with `closed_at: null`, and the same sentence with
  `40400` in it with `FACTORY_CLOSE_FIRED_S=120`. The review names a fifth thing the shipped read cannot
  see: a pull request is also an issue to the REST API, so `issues/282` answers `state: closed` with a
  real `closed_at`, and #292's body says `its fix merged as #282 at 11:01:37Z on 11 Nov` -- a verb aimed
  at a merged sibling. Measured here: `gh issue view 282 --json state` answers `MERGED`, and the raw REST
  read that would show the discriminator is refused in this session
  (`gh api repos/vicowa-botworks/parental-lockout/issues/282` prints `Permission denied: shell`, #1180's
  first failure class), so the field is pinned by a planted payload rather than a live call.
- Options: `scan($re)` for the numbers, one verdict helper behind both arms, one probe wait per batch, and
  a kind field read in the same call as the state | keep `capture` and light the legs the review counted
  | three `api_get` calls per artifact, state then timestamp then kind | delimit the triple with a tab, as
  the harness's other stubs do | pass a verb aimed at a pull request in silence | leave the sleep in the
  loop and set `FACTORY_CLOSE_PROBE=0` in the legs
- Chose: `scan($re)` for the numbers, one verdict helper behind both arms, one probe wait per batch, and a
  kind field read in the same call as the state
- Why: a reader that reports what it pattern-matched instead of what the artifact says, four times over.
  `capture` reports the first number on a line, so keeping it and adding legs would be a coverage fix for
  a correctness fault: the pass names a ticket the verb never pointed at and never reads the one it did,
  and its verdict is a comment written on that artifact. Three calls per artifact was what the surrounding
  code already did for state and timestamp, and it is wrong at three: two reads of one ticket can
  straddle a write, so a delta built from the state before a close and the timestamp after it is a delta
  nobody observed -- one jq filter, one read, one instant. A tab as the separator was rejected on
  measurement, not taste: tab is IFS *whitespace*, so `IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c` over
  `OPEN<tab><tab>ISSUE` answers `a=OPEN b=ISSUE c=` -- an open ticket's kind lands in its timestamp and
  the kind is empty, the one artifact the branch exists to distinguish; both spellings were run and
  U+001F is not whitespace. Silently passing a verb aimed at a pull request was rejected because it is a
  real finding about the body -- the author pointed the keyword at something no closer acts on -- and a
  silent pass is exactly how #353 began, with nobody saying what the merge had done. Leaving the sleep in
  the loop was rejected because the finding is a count: a body naming five open tickets held
  `factory_merge` for fifty seconds before the worktree cleanup ran, on every merge, for a reason -- the
  closer's seconds-long asynchrony -- that belongs to the batch, not to each ticket. Measured cost of the
  four: 2 wrong numbers out of 2 test lines, 2 false healthy verdicts, 40 s of wall clock per bad merge,
  and one misattributed note waiting on a merged sibling.
- Affects: `factory/factory.sh` -- `factory_close_read` and `factory_close_verdict` are new, the scan in
  `factory_verify_closure` says `scan($re)` where it said `capture(...)`, the loop is two passes with one
  `sleep` between them, and the note-building arm is unchanged bytes. `factory/selftest.sh` -- the lift
  takes one awk span instead of two `sed` ranges that each stopped at the first `^}` (the two new helpers
  sit between the old ranges, and the fixture already documents being bitten once by a helper the lift
  forgot, so all three are asserted now); the `run_action` stub gains a `fail-note` switch, because an
  always-succeeding stub leaves `CLOSE-NOTE-FAILED` unlit; the `Refs`/`Part of` leg asserts
  `[ ! -e "$2/calls" ]` where it grepped a file the healthy path never creates and counted its own `No
  such file or directory` as the pass; ten legs are new. `docs/factory.md` and
  `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` carry the same finding in prose, the latter naming the merge-time
  read as the supervisor's second ask.
- Reproduction: the ten new legs are: one verb over two numbers verdicts both; a verb verdicts the number
  it touches, not the first on the line; a verb aimed at a pull request is named and gets no issue
  verdict; a close that lands during the re-probe with no clock is UNTIMED; one 40400 s late is LATE; a
  state that is neither answer on the first read; the same after the re-probe; no `merged_at` skips in
  words; a close that predates the merge keeps its negative delta; a note that cannot be written is
  journalled. Plus one text leg: exactly one `sleep` in the function, on the batch line. The fifth arm the
  review counted -- `scan_state = failed` -- stays dark on purpose and says so where it stands: it fires
  only when `jq` fails on a well-formed body, and the only way to make that happen here breaks the body
  read too, landing the run in `CLOSE-CHECK-SKIPPED` instead. The misattribution is re-runnable in one
  line: `CLOSER_RE=$(grep -m1 '^CLOSER_RE=' factory/factory.sh | cut -d"'" -f2); printf '%s\n' '#7 is the
  reason. Fixes #12.' | jq -Rsr --arg re "$CLOSER_RE" '[scan($re) | .[0]]'` answers `["12"]` -- the
  capture group, so bare digits -- and the same pipeline over `Closes #301 and Closes #304.` answers
  `301 304`, where the shipped `capture` answered `301`.
- Refs: #353 (the ticket this component exists for), #357 (the review), H-0157 (the pass's first shape),
  H-0164 (the pattern it reads), #1180 (read the artifact; the raw REST refusal above is quoted, not
  inferred), #1807 (the gate ran alone in this worktree, no mutation sweep in flight).
- Checkpoint: f20cb35
- Effect: the checkpoint is an empty commit whose tree is `8c9999b`, so it holds the pass exactly as the
  review read it. Its ordering is stated rather than hidden: it was taken after the edits were drafted,
  which means it records the pre-decision bytes by content, not by position in the history. `git revert
  f20cb35..HEAD` returns `capture`, the duplicated verdict and the in-loop sleep. Gate, each command

  `python3 scripts/check-scripts.py`, `python3 scripts/check-close-verb.py --self-test` -> `18 fixtures,
  every class where the parser says it is`, exit 0, `bash factory/selftest.sh`, and `make verify` ->
  `verify: OK`, exit 0.

## H-0166 · Nothing ever read a commit message, and this branch's own carried two verbs GitHub may honour: the write side is made stricter than the read side on purpose, and published history is adjudicated in a file rather than rewritten

- Question: #357's review asked for a rule about what a writer may put beside an issue number. H-0164
  built that rule into `scripts/check-close-verb.py` and it reads FILES -- a body handed to it at review
  time. The question this entry answers is what protects the text nobody hands to it: the commit messages
  on the same branch, which GitHub parses the same way and acts on when the commit reaches the default
  branch. Measured on this branch before anything was changed: `git log --format=%B origin/main..HEAD`
  at `17b37c7`, read with the WIDE claim scan -- a verb, then the nearest following number, the width
  `CLAIM_RE` carries -- answered `Closing -> #77` and `Resolving -> #78` in `8c9999b`, in the sentence
  written to WARN about the hazard, which is PR #245's shape from #1256 reproduced one layer down. The
  tight adjacency regex and the checker as shipped both answered nothing on the same bytes, because the
  number sits after a line break; that is the width question from the other side, and it is why the
  report prints the verb it refused. The live read
  says #77 is `MERGED` (closedAt 2026-10-17T00:00:04Z) and #78 `CLOSED` (2026-10-16T15:00:51Z), both
  closed long before the message was written, so that merge would have changed nothing: luck about two
  numbers, not a property of the shape. The open question underneath is what to DO about it, because the
  message is already pushed.
- Options: refuse undocumented inflections at WRITE time -- a fifth class in the checker, a span-blind
  scan of every message between the base and HEAD inside `make verify`, and a waiver file for claims that
  are already published, exact on sha and number set and reprinted on every run -- while the read side
  keeps the documented nine | widen the read-side `CLOSER_RE` to the `-ing` forms too, so both engines
  agree on one superset | report undocumented forms in messages as advice and exit 0, so the gate stays
  green and the reader is told | rewrite `8c9999b` so the branch is clean and no waiver is needed
- Chose: refuse undocumented inflections at WRITE time -- a fifth class in the checker, a span-blind scan
  of every message between the base and HEAD inside `make verify`, and a waiver file for claims that are
  already published, exact on sha and number set and reprinted on every run -- while the read side keeps
  the documented nine
- Why: the two sides fail in opposite directions and only one of them touches an artifact. The read side,
  `factory_verify_closure`, writes its verdict ONTO a live ticket, so a pattern that reaches too far
  writes a false sentence on somebody's issue -- that is exactly what H-0164 measured (a 20-character
  window invented 15 closers across the merged corpus) and why the read side stays narrow. The write side
  costs a reworded sentence when it says no, and an unplanned close when it says yes. Given one form --
  `Closing #77` -- whose behaviour is genuinely unknown here, the narrow question and the strict question
  are both right, in their own place. What is NOT known is whether GitHub honours an `-ing` verb, and
  this corpus cannot answer it: all 180 merged bodies contain ONE adjacent `-ing` specimen, PR #47's
  `closing #46`, and that body also carries the documented `Closes #46.` two lines later -- one
  observation, confounded, so #46 closing 2 s after the merge proves nothing about the `-ing` line. So
  the write side refuses it without claiming it fires, and says so in the report ("whether it fires is
  unmeasured here, so it is refused"). The superset option is refused because it imports the invented-claim
  defect into the side that writes. The advisory option is refused because it is the state that let the specimen
  through: a warning in a log nobody reads is what a green gate already is. The rewrite option is refused before it is
  weighed -- AGENTS.md permits only `git revert`, force-pushing an in-flight branch is forbidden, and
  this repository has `allow_squash_merge=false` and `allow_rebase_merge=false` (#1264), so a merged
  message is permanent history either way.
- Affects: `scripts/check-close-verb.py` -- `KEYWORDS`, `HAZARD`, the `hazard` class in `classify`, a
  `spans` switch (the inertness of a code span is a measurement made over BODIES, 0 fired of 2, and has
  never been made over messages, so a message is read span-blind), a `-` path meaning stdin, and
  `--span-blind`; `scripts/check-commit-verbs.sh` is new; `Makefile` gains `==> commit-message claims`
  in the `verify:` recipe; `factory/close-verb-waivers` is new, with one entry, for `8c9999b`;
  `factory/selftest.sh` gains seven legs; `docs/factory.md` and the factory SKILL carry the rule.
  `factory/factory.sh` is deliberately NOT changed: its nine keywords are correct for what it does.
- Reproduction: `git log --format=%B origin/main..HEAD | python3 scripts/check-close-verb.py --span-blind
  -` exits 1 and prints `REFUSED, NOT A KEYWORD #77, #78`, naming its own motivating specimen; the same

## H-0168 · PR #354's collision puts both sides' sentences in the SAME paragraph of `triage.sh`'s usage text, so the proof that both intents survived cannot be a line diff, and the log's placement is the gate's call for the fourth time on this hazard

- Question: Where does a conflict resolution get its order from, and what counts as evidence that both sides' work is still in the tree, when `git merge origin/main` halts on TWO files at once -- the decision log, and one paragraph of `factory/triage.sh`'s `--help` text that BOTH sides extended? (#354, `issue-313` at `5710cfb`, `origin/main` `aac8218`: `CONFLICTING`/`DIRTY` with every check green.)

- Options: edit the two conflict hunks in the conflicted files until the gate goes green | splice `factory/DECISIONS.md` out of the two parent blobs at byte-exact boundaries and let `scripts/check-decisions.py`'s ascending-id rule place this branch's block, keeping `triage.sh`'s paragraph as a word union | move the branch instead of merging -- rebase, or squash and force-push onto `main`, so no merge commit exists to resolve | take `--theirs` for `factory/triage.sh`, because the class list on the line above already prints `parked` and the sentence repeats a fact the table states | re-point every coordinate the merge moves, so the record is internally consistent at the merge commit

- Escalated: no

- Refers: H-0142, H-0143, H-0144, H-0155, H-0159, H-0161

- Why: Option 3 is not a move a unit has and not one this repository survives: force-push is denied to a tick by `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, and `AGENTS.md` records that `allow_squash_merge` and `allow_rebase_merge` are both false here, so the only merge available is a merge commit whose history is permanent. A conflict therefore has to be resolved forward, and the whole question is what the resolution is and how it is proved. Option 1 is refused on the standing ground -- a conflict hunk is git's guess about alignment (`H-0142`'s cut, kept by `H-0145`, `H-0152`, `H-0161`) -- and the guess was measured here rather than quoted: git put this branch's whole 18-line `H-0155` block on one side of `main`'s five-entry block (`H-0154`, `H-0157`, `H-0158`, `H-0159`, `H-0161`, 422 lines) in ONE hunk at line 7281, which offers exactly two orders and calls neither of them a verdict. The order is the gate's: `scripts/check-decisions.py:236` "%s: %s is out of order (%s came before it); the log is a history" refuses an entry whose number sits below its predecessor's, so `H-0155` fits in one place only, between `H-0154` (`main`'s heading 7281) and `H-0157` (7331). Both orders were run, not asserted: the splice below answers `155 entries across 1 log(s)` and exit 0, while the same bytes with this branch's block appended after `main`'s last heading answer `:7736: H-0155 is out of order (H-0161 came before it); the log is a history and a history that jumps around cannot be bisected` and exit 1. Option 4 is refused by tie-break 3 -- a refusal to proceed on input that is missing beats a quieter file -- applied to a merge, where the missing input is somebody else's sentence. It is also wrong on its own facts: the paragraph is where `triage.sh --help` explains the `detail` column, `main`'s sentence explains the two marks that do NOT change the class and this branch's explains the one class whose detail names the label it read, they qualify different values of the same column, and the paragraph carries both. ## H-0169 · The ranking key reads the clock once per row, so a second boundary between two reads calls the later stamp the older one and dispatches the young unit first

- Id: this entered the harness log as `H-0157` on `issue-302`, allocated by `factory/next-decision-id.sh` at `7f3edbd`, 2026-11-13T19:26:33-05:00.
