  to a maintainer

- Why: #393 reserved this exact call -- "The ratchet question for that new class is the user's, not a
  unit's ... so a unit that lands the check should land it as a report-only list first and say how many
  rows it finds" -- so the shape is asked for, not inferred. The count is why the refusal is not:
  measured at `origin/main` `25d290478`, 152 citations name 22 ids with no heading in either log, and 21
  of the 22 have no heading on ANY ref this clone holds (`refs/heads` and `refs/remotes` both swept),
  `H-0122` on `backup-tip` being the exception. Read as classes rather than as a number: 79 citations of
  11 ids are fixture names quoted as evidence of a measurement (`D-0001`-`D-0010`, `D-0020`, `D-9999`),
  never meant to be entries; 35 of 4 are the documented holes and the documented renumber (`H-0031`,
  `H-0032`, `H-0057`, `D-0027`), each explained in prose on trunk; 31 of 3 are the allocator-race ids
  named inside the very entries that explain the gap (`H-0260`, `H-0262`, `H-0277`); 4 of 3 are prose
  about a collision resolved by renumbering (`D-0091`, `D-0094`, `D-0099`); and 3 of 1 is `H-0122`, the
  stranded record that opened the issue. (a) turns every branch red the day it ships, including the one
  landing it, and sets a constant over a corpus whose largest class is fixture prose. (c) is the silence
  the issue names -- count unchanged, exit 0, the pointer false forever. (d) is what the class ends at,
  but not here: a report refuses nothing and publishes nothing, so nothing irreversible happens while it
  waits, and the number it prints is what the maintainer needs in order to decide.

  stranded id necessarily names it: `H-0316` took three citations of `H-0122` out of the log and the prose
  that explains the re-aim cites it again, so the census books the repair as a dangling mention. Read this
  report against `origin/main` `25d290478`, where it is 152 and 22, and not against the branch repairing
  it, where the entries that repair it keep it alive -- its floor is the number of records that explain the
  gaps, not zero, and the sentence says `Reported, not refused` so the number cannot be read as a verdict.
  A `#`-qualified mention (`backup-tip:factory/DECISIONS.md#H-0122`) is exempt by design, which makes

- Confidence: high on the mechanism -- one leg plants the mention and requires a green run that names the
  id, and requires the same fixture without the mention to say nothing at all; re-running the leg against
  the gate as it stood at the previous checkpoint makes it fail on the planted id, so the leg measures the
  sentence rather than the fixture. Medium on the classification above: the 22 ids and their counts are
  machine-read, which class each one belongs to is my reading of the prose around it, and the line prints
  all 22 so a reader can disagree without re-deriving anything.
- Revisit: the number this prints is the number a `POINTER_DEBT`-shaped constant would take, and that is
  the user's call (#374 argues the ratchet forbids debt rising without obliging it to fall). When it is
  set, the fixture-id class and the `#` exemption have to be decided in the same breath or the constant

## H-0319 · Three decision records live on refs no pull request has ever had, and the one repair that fits `D-0053` is publishing someone else's dropped branch

- Question: `D-0053` and the navigation `D-0015` live only on `wip/issue-204-dropped-6bfd528`, and
  `D-0019` only on `wip/issue-211-dropped-1df729a`; neither ref has a pull request in any state. `D-0053`'s
  own `Chose:` is "deliver the branch unchanged as an open pull request that records the drop", and there is
  no such pull request. What does a unit do?
- Options: (a) open both pull requests itself as drafts -- the act records the drop and merges nothing |
  (b) re-open #204 so the queue sees the gap | (c) comment on the issue and take no write action |
  (d) escalated to a maintainer
- Chose: escalated to a maintainer
- Why: `AGENTS.md:52` "naming what is owed, and stop" -- and the instruction above it names the class: the
  four decisions not an agent's to make are a third-party dependency, security or tamper-resistance
  semantics, publishing, and deleting data. Opening a pull request whose commits are another unit's dropped
  work is publishing, and this repository's policy makes the consequence concrete rather than
  hypothetical: the factory never merges without an approving review, so the only durable thing an agent
  can create here is a standing request a named human must dispose of, under an agent's name, on a branch
  its own author marked `do not merge` in the one case where that was written down (`#285`, the
  `backup-tip` copy). (a) is exactly what `D-0053` chose for itself and never executed five weeks ago,
  which argues the maintainer should execute it, not that an agent should do it unasked. (b) re-opens #204,
  measured `CLOSED` at `2026-11-09T17:11:02Z`, and a re-open is a queue-visible state change on an issue
  whose UI asks are being worked by #387 -- a unit inventing work for another unit is not a repair. (c) is
  the fallback this entry in fact does, but not as the whole answer: a comment leaves nothing in the
  repository that says these refs are load-bearing, which is the actual hazard.

## H-0322 · A unit's own probe fixtures halted the whole queue from inside its own worktree: does the scratch location live in the tree behind an ignore rule, in prose that says `/tmp`, in a wider content verdict, or in a directory the dispatch mints outside the tree and tears down at session end?

- Question: where may a unit write throwaway fixtures -- probe repositories, fake trees, anything
  written to answer a question and thrown away -- so they cannot hold the queue hostage? Measured for
  this entry in the supervisor's own journal: 39 `HALTED`-family lines name `wt/issue-328`, from
  `2026-11-15T18:51:41Z` (`CONFLICT-HALTED pr:398`) to `2026-11-16T02:31:09Z`, whose own words record
  the cause already `7h39m` old; the dirt was eight untracked `.probe/*` directories, several of them
  nested `git init` repositories, written by the unit whose deliverable was already approved when the
  halt fired.
- Options: (a) a `.scratch/` convention inside each tree with an ignore rule -- `.git/info/exclude`,
  committed `.gitignore`, or `core.excludesFile` -- offered as pre-clean advice | (b) prose only: the
  skill says `/tmp` and nothing else changes | (c) widen the content verdict to treat dot-prefixed
  or named scratch shapes as non-load-bearing | (d) the dispatch mints one per-tick directory outside
  every worktree, exports `$FACTORY_SCRATCH`, names it in the tick's own prompt, and deletes it when
  the session ends, with the skill bullet and the halt sentence carrying the rule and the resume trap
- Chose: (d) the dispatch mints one per-tick directory outside
  every worktree, exports `$FACTORY_SCRATCH`, names it in the tick's own prompt, and deletes it when
  the session ends, with the skill bullet and the halt sentence carrying the rule and the resume trap
- Why: (a) fails on the ground the halt itself rests on: an in-tree directory stays invisible only
  while an ignore rule says so, and the content verdict refuses to guess about untracked bytes
  because guessing in the wrong direction destroys work nobody else holds (the #228 verdict;
  `AGENTS.md` repeats it for `git worktree --force`, "refuses a dirty tree and `--force` answers
  'you are sure', never 'someone is home'"). An ignore is also untracked state -- a stale or missing
  rule reinstates the halt, and #328 and #414 are the second and third times this repository met the
  same trap. (b) has no janitor: a tick killed mid-run leaves its `/tmp` fixtures forever, and
  nothing in the harness ever learns where they are. (c) guesses about work that is nowhere else --
  exactly what the verdict exists to refuse. (d) removes the failure mode instead of adjudicating
  it: bytes outside every tree are invisible to no census because no census looks there, nothing has
  to be ignored, and the teardown makes the fixtures die with the tick that made them, including the
  killed one. It is still advisory by construction -- the halt stays the backstop for a unit that
  litters its tree anyway -- which is why the same commit teaches the rule in
  `.opencode/skills/factory/SKILL.md` and the prompt itself, and why the halt sentence now names the
  resume trap this ticket exposed: `git clean -fd` refuses to touch a directory containing a
  `.git`, so over exactly the fixture shape that halted the queue the documented dry run prints one
  line -- `Would skip repository .probe/a`, exit 0, no `Would remove` line for `.probe/` itself,
  nothing removed -- and an operator who counts `Would remove` paths and trusts the exit removes the
  marker and re-halts on the same bytes. Measured on this box's git 2.53.0: the plain run over the
  plant said only the skip line and `git status` still held `?? .probe/` after it;
  `clean -ffd -n` said `Would remove .probe/`. A first draft of this entry claimed the plain run
  printed 0 paths, then that it echoed the honest line beside the skip -- both refuted by re-running
  the probe and reading its bytes; the leg's premise checks the absence of a `Would remove` line,
  which is what the plant actually shows. The leg
  appended in `factory/selftest.sh` below every cited line re-measures that premise from the plant
  on every suite run and fails the suite, naming the plant's own output, if the git on the box ever
  stops honouring it.
- What it lost: (a) would have kept scratch next to the work, visible to the unit's own `git status`
  and reviewable in the tree where it was written, at the price of an ignore rule that must never be
  stale; (c) would have absorbed a whole class of halt without any prose change at all, and with it
  went the safety of never guessing -- a real half-finished deliverable in a dot-directory is
  indistinguishable from scratch by name, and a verdict that guessed "scratch" and ticked on is the
  work lost silently instead of loudly. (d)'s own cost: scratch is now one `cd` away from the tree
  rather than inside it, the unit sees only a sentence telling it so, and with `mktemp` refused the
  pass can only journal `SCRATCH-FAILED` and dispatch without the sentence.
- Confidence: high on the state, each row re-read for this entry -- the 39 journal lines and their
  two endpoints are `grep -h 'HALTED' factory/log/supervisor.log* | grep -c 'issue-328'` and its
  first and last rows, and the 7h39m figure is the halt sentence's own words in the last of them,
  matching the ticket title; a first unverified figure (173 lines) written before measuring was
  caught by exactly that grep and corrected here. Medium on coverage: (d) fences the scratch a
  dispatched tick is told about; a human working in a unit's tree, or a unit that ignores the
  sentence, still reaches the halt -- by design, because that dirt really is nowhere else.
- Revisit: if a dispatched unit is next halted for fixtures inside its tree, the sentence and the
  bullet were not enough and the next options are (a) plus (c) together -- pre-clean with a
  provisioned rule AND a verdict arm that at least names the shape in the halt -- or the mint gains

## H-0323 · The #364 guard counted `mktemp` on code lines at zero and this branch's own scratch mint is one: do we un-mint the scratch, re-tune the guard to count invocations, or widen the guard away?

- Question: when a later pass legitimately introduces into `factory/factory.sh` a call shape an
  earlier pass's selftest leg had pinned to zero, which of the two is wrong, and what does the leg
  say now? Measured on this branch's head `ac0b849`: the CI `shellcheck` job died at three findings
  (two SC1003, with SC1117 following, on the `scr415_env_channel` mutant strings, and SC2034 on a
  `FACTORY_LEDGER` assignment in the H-0322 halt-box fixture) and stopped every job under it, and
  the selftest underneath it answered `909 passed, 1 failed` — `FAIL both arms name one stream`.
  That leg counts mktemp occurrences on code lines — every line that does not open with `#` — and
  requires 0, and the shipped `factory/factory.sh:1376` "scratch=$(mktemp -d" mints the per-tick
  scratch under `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}` — deliberately shipped by this branch's own H-0322. The leg
  was not broken: it guards the shape #364 was about, and the pre-#364 stream arms spelled their
  paths `$(mktemp …)`, so "no code line says mktemp" had been a free proxy for "no arm names its
  own stream" only while no other legitimate `mktemp` existed in the file.
- Options: (a) un-mint: name the scratch deterministically under `$FACTORY_RUN` and keep the leg's
  zero | (b) keep the mint and re-tune the leg to count the invocation shape `$(mktemp` on code
  lines, exactly one, and pin that one by the mint's own fixed string `scratch=$(mktemp -d` — the
  exception as a ledger, not a hole | (c) drop the mktemp count from the leg and rest on the two
  `factory_worktree_stream` counts | (d) a location-scoped exemption: the leg ignores mktemp lines
  inside the scratch block
- Chose: (b) keep the mint and re-tune the leg to count the invocation shape `$(mktemp` on code
  lines, exactly one, and pin that one by the mint's own fixed string `scratch=$(mktemp -d` — the
  exception as a ledger, not a hole
- Why: the two shellcheck findings were fixed in the commit ahead of the checkpoint because that
  job gates every check under it; (a) buys the blunt zero by re-implementing `mktemp -d`: a deterministic name needs its own
  exists-check, and the race handling that check needs is the logic `mktemp` ships and this
  repository chose not to own; and the scratch is no stream, so the sweep-match the rename would
  have to dodge is protection for nothing the guard asked about. (c) removes exactly the protection
  #364 bought — the leg's own words: a stream written outside the swept directory is "the whole of
  #364" — and every stream leg above stays green under a renamed `$(mktemp …)` stream arm, because
  their markers come from the arms' own writing and follow a rename. (d) has no single-occurrence
  property: one exemption inside a block silently permits a second inside the same block. (b) keeps
  the two countable facts: neither stream arm names its own file (both

## H-0327 · A conflict fetch that fails defers with a pointer to a line that says nothing — is the cause written into the deferral's own sentence, into the FAILED line it points at, as a classification of the exit code, or by fixing the transport?

- Question: `CONFLICT-DEFERRED pr:405 … the reason is the line above` pointed at
  `FAILED (128) git -C <tree> fetch origin main`, and git answers 128 for a revoked key, a deleted
  repository, a full disk and a TCP timeout alike — remedies unrelated to each other, and the queue
  cannot tell which it waited on. Measured 16 Nov: five of eight conflict units deferred on one
  SSH-22 burst, 135 s a pop — 11m15s of a 5400 s budget — while `gh` merged over HTTPS seconds
  later on the same content (#417). The cause existed in the tick log, not the journal; and git's
  LAST line in that burst was `Please make sure you have the correct access rights`, the sentence
  that sends an operator hunting a rotated deploy key while the first line — `ssh: connect to host
  github.com port 22: Connection timed out` — named the real thing. Where does the cause go, and
  what bounds the wait?
- Options: (a) fix the line the pointer names — teach `run_action` to carry the failed command's
  first stderr line into every `FAILED` row, so every action's failure self-explains |
  (b) quote git's first stderr line verbatim into the deferral's own sentence under the harness's
  `git said:` marker, and run the fetch behind `FACTORY_FETCH_TIMEOUT` like the refresh arm's
  activation fetch |
  (c) classify the failure into cause tokens (transport / credentials / missing) and journal the
  classification instead of git's words |
  (d) change the transport — port 443 of `ssh.github.com` in the machine's `~/.ssh/config`
- Chose: (b) quote git's first stderr line verbatim into the deferral's own sentence under the
  harness's `git said:` marker, and run the fetch behind `FACTORY_FETCH_TIMEOUT` like the refresh
  arm's activation fetch
- Why: (a) rewrites every `FAILED` row in the journal for one arm's need, and it cannot be written
  honestly where it sits: `run_action` journals the command's true rc but answers a normalized
  `return 1` — measured while building this fix, when my first clause quoted `(1)` for a real 128
  because it read the return value instead of the journalled rc; the selftest control caught it.
  (c) contradicts the harness's own doctrine — `factory_git_said` and the `git said:` marker exist
  precisely to carry git's wording without paraphrasing it (`factory_git_incomplete`'s comment:
  "what this does NOT do is look at what git said"), and a classification is a paraphrase that
  goes stale silently on the first re-wrapped git message. (d) is a machine-level edit the issue
  itself says is not a unit's write from a tick. Within (b), the FIRST line is the cause and the
  LAST is the decoy — the fixture scripts both lines and the leg asserts the decoy's absence — and
  a 128 with no parseable cause still carries git's sentence, which beats a pointer. The bound:
  the ticket asked for `ssh -o ConnectTimeout=15`, and `FACTORY_FETCH_TIMEOUT` is the constant
  H-0075 already ruled every network read in a lock-holding pass rides behind — the refresh arm
  three screens above states its can-it-hurt (a killed fetch is 124, leaves no `.lock`, costs
  seconds), and it bounds the whole call rather than only the TCP handshake; this fetch was the
  one network read on the conflict path that had been missed. A parked connection writes nothing
  before it dies — measured at /tmp/opencode/pk417: `timeout … 10 git fetch` over a stub that
  parks 5 s answers rc 124 at 10.0 s with EMPTY stderr, and the ssh record shows TWO invocations,
  git retries a failed ssh once, so one burst costs 2x the park — so 124/137 with an empty stream
  is itself a cause sentence: `killed at the …s fetch bound with nothing written`. Removing
  `run_action` from this call is part of the choice, not collateral: it answers 1 for every failed
  command, and this arm must tell the parked connection (124) from git's own 128 to pick which
  sentence to write; the `ACTION`/`FAILED` pair is journalled here in the shape the refresh arm
  already gives its fetch.
- What it lost: (a) would make every failed action self-explaining in one line and needed no

## H-0332 · #483's census bounded the scan's reads and declared "every harness-owned git call", yet the conflict arm's mirror push — the one network WRITE a pass makes — still had no deadline and fails in exactly the shape #419 measured: share the fetch's constant, give the write its own bound and cause-naming arm, tune ssh instead of the wrapper, or move the push outside the pass?

- Question: #419's measured incident is a fetch parked for 98 minutes, but the same conflict arm
  ends with `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/$branch` behind no wrapper at all — measured here
  before any edit: at trunk `49f7fa1`+ the arm read `run_action git -C "$tree" push origin
  "HEAD:refs/heads/$branch"`, and #483's own decision text claims the census covered every
  harness-owned git network call. A parked receive-pack costs the queue the same 135 s-a-pop the
  fetch cost, inside the same lock and the same budget, and the incident pass ran both the read
  and the write of that arm inside the one window that ate 5400 s. `run_action` also answers 1 for
  every failed command, so the arm could not tell a killed push (124) from git's own refusal (128)
  even if a bound existed. What is owed the write, and what may NOT change about it?
- Options: (a) reuse `FACTORY_FETCH_TIMEOUT` for the push — one constant, one knob |
  (b) give the write its own `FACTORY_PUSH_TIMEOUT` beside the fetch constant in
  `factory/common.sh`, wrap the push in `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=5` exactly like the
  fetch arm's, and leave `run_action` for a cause-naming arm that keeps the stderr in a swept
  stream (`factory_push_stream`) and writes the `git said:` / bound sentences the fetch arm writes
  |
  (c) tune ssh instead of the wrapper — `-c core.sshCommand='ssh -o ConnectTimeout=15
  -o ServerAliveInterval=15 -o ServerAliveCountMax=2'` (the ticket's own repair 1) |
  (d) move the push outside the serialized pass so no parked write holds the lock
- Chose: (b) give the write its own `FACTORY_PUSH_TIMEOUT` beside the fetch constant in
  `factory/common.sh`, wrap the push in `timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=5` exactly like the
  fetch arm's, and leave `run_action` for a cause-naming arm that keeps the stderr in a swept
  stream (`factory_push_stream`) and writes the `git said:` / bound sentences the fetch arm writes
- Why: (a) merges two knobs whose worst cases can part — a slow-but-live link may deserve a
  different allowance for a write than for a read, and a rename that re-points a bound later must
  not silently move the other one; they share the DEFAULT (120) because a parked write costs the
  queue what a parked read costs, which is a measurement, not a merged name.
  (c) does not cover the whole park: `ConnectTimeout` bounds connection establishment only, and
  #417 measured parks whose first ssh attempt never wrote a line at all — `timeout` is the only
  wrapper that answers with an rc (`124`) no command of ours produced and names itself in the
  journal; and H-0327 already retired a transport-retuning option for the same reason — the fix
  must live where the harness can journal it.
  (d) is a correctness loss dressed as a latency win: the merge and its mirror push are one
  serialized act; pushing from outside the pass lets a second activation re-merge the same branch
  against a different `origin/main` while the first push is still parked, which is a split-brain
  mirror, and #419 asked for a bound, not a new writer.
  The verdicts the arm already made stay: a failed push is `CONFLICT-UNPUSHED`, return 2, retried
  next activation — the legs pin that naming the cause changed nothing about the deferral.
  What loses: a live-but-slow link whose push needs more than 120 s now fails and defers (the
  same thing the fetch has said since #483); a pass's worst case per conflicted branch grows from
  one bound to two (fetch + push, 240 s shipped), which is why both are journalled as `ACTION`
  before they start — a death between the two lines names which one was in flight; and the bound
  cannot distinguish a parked connection from a receive-pack legitimately busy with a huge push,

## H-0333 · #419's killed pass left 1h39m of silence with no `END rc=` at all, and a reader could not tell a death from a pass that never started: journal the death from inside the pass, infer it from activation boundaries outside, journal only the budget overrun, or accept the silence?

- Question: the incident row reads `1h39m with zero journal lines, no END rc, 0 units worked`.
  Every verdict in the journal is written by the planned path at the end of `factory_body`, so a
  pass stopped by systemd's start deadline — or by anything else that signals — dies between its
  last `NEXT` row and the END, leaving the two states (killed, never-started) with identical
  evidence. A repair exists for the slow half (#419 repair 1, `H-0332`) but a bounded pass can
  still outlive its budget, and the queue still gets no sentence explaining the gap. Measured on
  this bash (5.3.9) before choosing: a trapped TERM handler runs and execution CONTINUES (the
  handler must exit by hand), and a lone EXIT trap registered with no TERM trap STILL FIRES on a
  default-TERM death with `$?` zero — so a half-armed trap writes `END rc=0` over a pass that
  died 143, a verdict-shaped lie in the worst direction, and the control leg exists to pin that.
  What must a dying pass write, and what may it never claim?
- Options: (a) journal only the self-inflicted case — check the budget before dispatch and write
  an overrun line — which says nothing when the deadline arrives mid-command from outside |
  (b) a death sentence from inside: register EXIT/TERM/INT/HUP traps in `factory_body` after the
  lock, write one final `END rc=<128+n> ticks_started=N died=<cause> inside=<unit> after=<n>s`
  through `log_event`, carry `died=` always so a death cannot read as a verdict, and disarm at
  both deliberate stops before their lines | (c) an outside sentinel — a later activation scans
  for a missing END and journals the inference — which survives even SIGKILL but quotes the dead
  pass through a clock it does not share and can never name the unit it was in |
  (d) teach `--status` readers to infer death from activation boundaries and write nothing.
- Chose: (b) a death sentence from inside: register EXIT/TERM/INT/HUP traps in `factory_body`
  after the lock, write one final `END rc=<128+n> ticks_started=N died=<cause> inside=<unit>
  after=<n>s` through `log_event`, carry `died=` always so a death cannot read as a verdict, and
  disarm at both deliberate stops before their lines
- Why: the pass is the only writer that knows, at the instant of dying, which unit it was in
  and how long it had been alive — `inside=` is unrecoverable by any later reader, and (c)'s
  inference would be the journal's only sentence built from another process's clock. `died=` is
  the contract: the `END rc=` token keeps its readers (the reap pair keys on activation
  boundaries, measured before this entry, not on the END text) while no death can ever wear the
  shape of a verdict, and the 128+n rc is the number `systemctl` and coreutils already print for
  the same death, so one incident shows the same figure in all three places. Registration sits
  after `flock` on purpose: the refused activation exits 7 having done nothing, and nothing must
  read as a death. Both measured bash semantics are load-bearing and pinned by legs, not prose:
  the TERM arm exits by hand because execution would otherwise continue after the handler
  (`factory/selftest.sh:27228` "a pass TERMed at its own push writes its own death sentence"),
  and the disarm precedes the planned END because the mutant that keeps only EXIT forges
  `END rc=0 died=EXIT` (`factory/selftest.sh:27291` "the death line is the traps"). Two silences no trap outruns are stated in the function instead
  of hidden: SIGKILL, and a stop inside a child that ignores TERM until the cgroup escalates —
  which is why the bounds of `H-0330` and `H-0332` are the precondition that makes the handler
  reachable at all.
- Follow-up: a SIGKILL survivor still writes no line, and no in-pass code can change that; if
  the queue ever shows a death with no `died=` row, that is the cgroup escalation outrunning the
  traps, and the next shape to reach for is (c)'s sentinel beside this one, not instead of it.
- Checkpoint: ca9444d3609f0cac28c72e6cc1df59118db6ebf1
